case_source: (From the judgement and order dated 14th of December, 2000 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4966 of 1998.
full_judgment:
Md Imman Ali J : This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 14-12-2000 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4966 of 1998 discharging the Rule.

2. The facts of the case, in brief, are that one Eklas Hossain Khan, predecessor of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed an implication under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.0206 acre of CS and SA Plot No. 565 appertaining to SA khatian No. 612 and mutation khatian No. 474/18. The case of the pre-emptor was that the case land along with other land originally belonged to Jogesh Chandra Majumder and others and the CS record of rights was accordingly prepared and published in their names. Golam Mortuza Khan, father of the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 3-11 purchased 5 kathas of land by registered deed of sale from the said tenants and lived there by constructing dwelling house and paid rents on mutation of his own name. Golam Mortuza Khan died leaving behind the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 3-5 as four sons and respondent Nos. 6-11 as six daughters and the said heirs possessed the land jointly by way of inheritance. Respondent No. 4 Golam Mostafa Khan by registered deed of sale dated 18-2-1988 transferred his share to his brother Moslemuddin Khan-respondent No. 3 and delivered possession. Respondent No. 3 transferred the said land by a deed of sale executed on the same date to the pre-emptee-Harunur Rashid and the deed of sale was registered on 13-8-1988. In spite of the fact that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the joint tenancy, no notice was served upon him. The pre-emptor was a stranger and a tenant under respondent No. 3. The pre-emptee declined to re-convey the land to the pre-emptor. Hence, the pre-emptor was constrained to make the application for pre-emption.

3. The pre-emptee appeared and opposed the application for pre-emption. His case was that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters got their inherited lands and properties amicably partitioned by a family arrangement executed on 5-5-1978. The case land was recorded in the name of Moslemuddin Khan, the vendor in the Dhaka Municipal Corporation in separate holding. The pre-emptor and his brothers and sister were paying rents in two separate jamas. The pre-emptee after purchase of the case land got his name mutated without any objection from any quarter in mutation khatian No. 474/18/1 and has been paying rent since then. The price of the land was settled at Taka 1,56,000 and the pre-emptee paid the said amount as consideration, but the price of the land was written as Taka 50,000. After purchase the pre-emptee had invested huge sum of money to construct a semi pucca building and obtained electricity, WASA and gas connection, thereby he had to incur a cost of Taka 1,15,000.

4. During the pendency of the pre-emption case the pre- emptor died leaving respondent Nos. 1 and 2 herein as his heirs and legal representatives.

5. On conclusion of hearing the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka dismissed the pre-emption application by his order dated 21-6-1998.

6. Being aggrieved, the pre-emptor prefer-red Miscellaneous Appeal No. 189 of 1998 and the said appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka, who by his judgement and order dated 18-11-1998 allowed the appeal thereby reversing the order passed by the trial Court, thus allowing the pre-emption.

7. Against the aforesaid judgement and order, the pre-emptee filed Civil Revision No. 4966 of 1998 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule, which upon hearing was dis-charged. Hence, the pre-emptee filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1008 of 2001 before this Division and leave was granted on the following submissions of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner:

“I. That in view of the concurrent finding of facts by the courts below including the High Court Division that "They are living separately", the High Court Division fell into error in "failing to note the distinction between co-sharers in the land transferred and co-sharer in the tenancy" inasmuch as even if the pre-emptors remain cosharer, in the tenancy but if they cease to be cosharer in the land transferred the right of preemption does not accrue and, as such, erred in holding that "So, the heirs of Golam Mortuza Khan must be held to be still enjoying the joint tenancy left by him" causing error in the decision of the case on its merit.

(II) That having regard to the provision of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. the High Court Division erred in holding that "Similarly, no amicable partition among the co-sharers even if reached in writing nor even a decree passed in a partition suit allowing different sharers to the co-sharers can substitute the order as mentioned in section 117 (c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act." And thereupon in allowing the case for pre-emption though it has been clearly found that the pre-emptors were no longer co-sharers in the land transferred. (See the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 239.

(III) That having regard to the fact that there has in fact been a separation of jama by Golam Mostafa Khan, an heir of Golam Mortuza Khan and thus the pre-emptors ceased to be joint tenant in respect of the land in question, a fact which could not be brought into evidence in the case (Annexed to the Leave Petition, this Court for doing complete justice in the case way look to the certified copy of the order of separation of tenancy in Mutation Case No.16511(Mir)/85 of Thana Revenue Officer, Tejgaon, Dhaka and/or pass an appropriate order for deciding the case completely and effectively."

8. Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He re-iterated that when the jama is separated by mutation, then an application for pre-emption cannot be maintained since the property ceases to be in joint ownership.

9. Mr Abut Kalam Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the respondent made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division. He further submitted that both the appellate Court as well as the High Court Division after thorough analysis and assessment of the pleadings and the evidence adduced by both the parties found that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the holding and the said pre-emption case was not barred by limitation and, as such, allowed the pre-emption case. He further submitted that the High Court Division found that no notice was ever served upon the heirs of Golam Mostafa Khan and no power of mutation has been given to any other authority including Dhaka Municipal Corporation; that mutation of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation to be valid must be based on an order in writing of the revenue authority concerned under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the Act); that the heirs of Golam Mostafa Khan are still enjoying the joint tenancy left by the father and that amicable partition amongst the co-sharers even if recorded in writing or even a decree passed in a partition suit, cannot subdivide the joint tenancy of Golam Mostafa Khan and, as such, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a cosharer in the tenancy left by him. He submitted that the High Court Division held that Exhibit. 'Uma (O)' series were issued during the pendency of hearing of the pre-emption case and that subdivision without notice upon a co-sharer of joint tenancy could not affect the right of pre-emption and admittedly both the appellate Court and High Court Division held that no notice was served upon the co-sharer for subdivision of the holding and, as such, the respondents are the co-sharers as well as the pre-emption was filed within time from the date of registration under section 60 of the Registration Act. He submitted that the Senior Assistant Judge committed error of law resulting in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the order dated 21-6-1998 in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.85 of 1988.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

11. In essence the only substantive issue is one of maintainability of the application for pre-emption of non- agricultural land under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act in the facts and circumstances of the case. The claim of the pre-emptor is that he is a co-sharer of the case plot by inheritance. In fact we find from the records that the vendor of the case land and the pre-emptor are full brothers. On the other hand, the claim of the pre-emptee is that the pre-emptor and his siblings are living separately having mutated their names in municipality records. The pre-emptee, therefore, claims that the pre-emptor and the vendor are no longer co-sharer. The learned Advocate for the appellants categorically submit-ted that by mutation, the property ceased to be in joint ownership and, therefore, the application for pre-emption cannot be maintained.

<u>12. On the question of maintainability of an application for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, reference has been made to the decision of this Division in the case of Aminullah (Md) vs Serajul Huq and others reported in 65 DLR (AD) 82, where three of us were party. In the said case it was held as follows:</u>

<u>"In a case of pre-emption filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy' Act if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be treated as co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. Therefore, in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian a co-sharer tenant can file a pre emption case under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. The words "one or more co-sharer tenants of such land" occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act means a co-sharer in the plot not the holding as mentioned in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act."</u>

<u>13. Moreover, the High Court Division elaborately discussed the provisions of section 117(1)(c) of the Act and observed that the Dhaka Municipal Corporation has not been given any authority under the said Act to effect mutation and that the authority under the said provision lies with the Revenue Officer. It was further observed that "separate holding number given by a Municipal Corporation cannot replace order an under section 117(1) (c) of the Act. So the heirs of Golam Mortuza Khan must be still enjoying the joint tenancy left by him. Similarly no amicable partition among the co-sharers even if reached in writing, nor even a decree passed in a partition suit allotting different shares to co-sharers can substitute the order as mentioned in section 117(1)(c) of the Act. The High Court Division agreed with the appellate Court that the joint tenancy was never divided and that thereby the pre-emptor did not cease to be a cosharer in the joint tenancy left by Golam Mortuza Khan.</u>

<u>14. We note further from the evidence on record that the pre-emptor is the full brother of the vendor of the case land. One should not lose sight of the intention of the legislature behind the provisions of law for pre-emption. Essentially the provision exists to prevent any stranger from buying land which form a part and parcel of jointly owned property. The aim of the legislature is to give opportunity to the co-sharers to buy the case land thereby excluding incursion by strangers. In the facts of the instant case, clearly the pre-emptor and the vendor being full brothers, the pre-emptor is entitled to prevent any stranger from entering into what was their joint family property. It has been rightly held that separation of the jama is not effective since the provisions of section 117(1)(c) of the Act have not been complied with; simply having a separate municipal holding does not sever the joint ownership of the property unless the mutation takes place in accordance with the provisions of the Act.</u>

15. In the facts and circumstances discussed above, we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgement.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without, however, any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties No. 1-4 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 30-9-2015 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal, in Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 2015 rejecting the appeal at the admission hearing upon affirming the judgment and order dated 1-9-2015 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gouranadi, Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No.25 of 2012 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus the present petitioner as pre-emptor filed the original preemption miscellaneous case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 against the pre-emptee and others in the Court of learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gournadi, Barisal contending inter alia that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case holding by way of inheritance and purchase. The pre-emptor came to learn about the case kabala for the first time on 26-5-2012. The opposite parties No.2-4 have transferred the case land secretly in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party No.1 without giving any notice to the pre-emptor-petitioner and thereafter; the pre-emptor collecting the certified copy of the deed in question on 28-5-2012, knowing finally about the sale in respect of the case land measuring 10 (ten) decimals at a consideration of Taka 3,00,000 (Three lac) filed the original case Apr getting the case land pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 as the purchaser-opposite party No.1 is a stranger to the case jote.

3. After service of summon-notice in the original case the pre- emptee-opposite party No.1 made his appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11(d) along with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the petition for pre-emption stated inter alia that the case is not maintainable in its present form as it is barred under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It was alleged by the pre-emptee that the nature of the case land is a homestead property and as such the petition for pre-emption is liable to be rejected.

4. Getting that application for rejection of the pre-emption case the pre-emptor filed a written objection contending inter alia that the application is not tenable in the eye of law and there is no scope to reject the petition for pre-emption under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

5. The learned trial court hearing the matter for rejection of the petition for pre-emption allowed the application filed by the pre-emptee-opposite party and by his order dated 1-9-2015 rejected the application for pre-emption.

6. Being aggrieved the pre-emptor preferred a Miscellaneous Appeal being No.64 of 2015 in the Court of learned District Judge, Barisal. The learned District Judge, Barisal at the very outset of the matter summarily rejected the miscellaneous appeal and affirmed the order passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gournadi, Barisal by the impugned judgment and order dated 30-9-2015.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the learned lower appellate court the pre-emptor-appellant-petitioner have preferred this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule.

8. During hearing of this Rule Mr Md Shahidul Islam, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mr Mohammad Noor Hossain, the learned Advocate appeared on behalf of the opposite parties.

9. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the learned appellate court below during passing the impugned order of rejection of the appeal summarily committed gross illegality and injustice. The learned Advocate further submits that both the courts below have committed error of law resulting in an error in the decisions occasioning failure of justice and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate also submits that the courts below have committed an error of law in not considering that the pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is changeable into a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural of Tenancy Act, 1949. The learned Advocate during his argument submits that section 2(14) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 i.e. the definition of non-agricultural land does not attract the case land and, as such, the pre-emption miscellaneous case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was maintainable. The learned Advocate in his submission pointed out that in the case land there is no existence of any dwelling but or homestead which is badly required for treating the lane as `Non-Agricultural Land', but the learned courts below erred in law as well as in facts and failed to appreciate the contents of the application for pre-emption which is the pleadings of the pre-emptor. Besides this; there is an Advocate Commissioner's report on the application for rejection of the case and the learned Advocate Commissioner in his report clearly mentioned that the land does not exist with homestead and it is a mere ‘Bhiti' land. The learned Advocate lastly submits that for misquoting or non-quoting of appropriate section in the contents of the application for pre-emption the right of pre-emption cannot be curtailed but the learned courts below arbitrarily decided that inasmuch as the original case was a case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 it is not maintainable and barred by law.

10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule submits that both the courts below during passing their judgment and order rightly held that the case is not maintainable as it is barred by law. The learned Advocate further submits that there is no illegality or infirmity and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submits that the Commissioner's report has no manner of application for consideration in such an application for rejection of plaint. Both the courts below concurrently held that the case land is under the purview of Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act, but since the miscellaneous application for pre-emption is under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it is barred by law.

11. Considering the submissions of the learned Advocates, I have perused the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 wherein it has been clearly contended by the pre-emptor-petitioner that the case land was transferred by a saf-kabala deed dated 28-5-2012 and the land measuring 10 decimals was transferred, in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1, who is a stranger purchaser at a consideration of Taka 3,00,000 (Taka three lac). The certified copy of the application for pre-emption is annexed herewith as Annexure-`A'. I have also consulted the application under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil' Procedure wherein it was cited by the opposite party No. 1 that the case land being a non-agricultural land and homestead the preemption miscellaneous case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 is not maintainable. With regard to this, having gone through the order passed by the trial court dated 1-9-2015 in pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 2012 and the order of the appellate court dated 30-9-2015 in Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 2015 it transpires that the learned District Judge, Barisal held that in the SA Khatian the land transferred, was mentioned as `Bhiti' and `Bagan' and for that reason it can be held that the land is not an agricultural land. In this context; section 2(14) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 defined the homestead in the following way:

"2(14) homestead' means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any courtyard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out-buildings used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purpose connected with agriculture or horticulture and such lands within well defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto."

12. Consulting the connected application it transpires that the provision of law under which the application for rejection of the preemption case was filed is under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Under this law, it is to be mentioned here that the plaint alone and not the application of the defendant shall be the basis of rejection of the plaint. To reject the plaint the court shall look into the case of the pre-emptor as set out in the plaint as a whole assuming all the averments therein to be correct.

13. Here in this case, we have come across from the contents of the plaint viz. the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the description of the property which was transferred in favour of the pre-emptee-opposite party is described as agricultural land. With regard to this, consulting the relevant case kabala being No.671 of 2012 dated 28-5-2012 it appears that in the schedule of the kabala there is a mention of Garden and "Bhita".

14. In the case of Ramchandra Saha vs Malay Baran Kundu, 24 BLD 280, this Court in paragraph No. 10 cited (quote):

The facts of the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 is, in short, that the pre-emptor petitioner filed an application under section 96 of the EB SAT Act for pre-emption of certain lands which was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties contending, inter alia, that the said land being "chandina land" within a Municipal area the application under section 96 of the Act had no application to the purchase in question. The case was allowed by the trial Court, which was affirmed by the subordinate Judge on appeal, preferred by the pre-emptee-opposite party. He then filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court Division and during pendency of the application a petition was filed on behalf of the pre-emptor under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 and section 153 of the CPC for amendment of the application for pre-emption whereby the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the SAT Act was sought to be converted to an application under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act which was rejected by the High Court on the ground that it would change the nature of the case. In an appeal against the said judgment and order by the pre-emptor the Appellate Division held that "In the circumstances we find that the learned judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. More-over, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title. "the Appellate Division also referred a decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR 347, PLD 1967 (Dacca) 588, in its Judgment where it was held that:—

"If the relief claimed by the petitioner was allowable under some other law of the country. Namely, section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then the Court of appeal below was bound to apply the same notwithstanding the mis-description of the cause title in the application."

<u>15. It is required to be mentioned that the land described in the schedule of the kabala shall prevail and it would be considered with the contents of the original plaint and it will govern the right of preemption. The spirit of law is such that the plaint or the application for pre-emption includes the kabala deed against which the pre-emptor preferred the application for pre-emption for getting the case land preempted. Hence, it is obvious to notes that at the time of taking consideration of the matter the court is under obligation to scrutinize the contents of the application for pre-emption as well as the contents of the case kabala.</u>

16. In the case of Abdul Majid Pramanik vs Md Sorhab Ali, 16 MLR (AD) 1, our Apex Court held with regard to section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 that the pre-emption of the land of homestead transferred by co-sharer of the tenancy situated in rural areas connected with agricultural, is not maintainable. Similarly, the land situated within municipal area although used for agricultural purpose, is pre-emptable under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

17. Our Appellate Division in the case of Jadav Chandra Mali vs Abdul Khaleque, 27 DLR (AD) 114 held.

"The pre-emptor wanted to exercise his right of pre-emption in respect of the disputed land on the ground that he was a co-sharer tenant of the tenancy to which the said land appertained. The application was described as one coming under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. Subsequently when it was realised that having regard to the nature of the disputed land the relief prayed for could be granted under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, an application for amendment to that effect in the cause title of the application with consequential changes was made but the High Court rejected the prayer on the ground inter alia, that the change sought to be made was not "a mere change of one kind of pre-emption to another ", but it was "substitution of a new case altogether." Since a co-sharer tenant of non-agricultural land and is entitled to apply for preemption under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, it does not appear how the nature and character of the application can be said to be altered by substitution of a new case altogether by reason of the amendment prayed for. Whatever changes were sought to be made were changes in form and not.in substance. In the circumstances we find that the learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the court under section 24 of the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title.

18. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and the discussions referred to above, I have the reason to have such a view that the learned lower appellate court during passing the impugned order dated 30-9-2015 in Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 2015 was not justified and legal in rejecting the Miscellaneous Case summarily affirming the order passed by the trial court. The earned District Judge, Barisal ought to have considered that the contents of the transfer deed is the basis of disposal of the application.

19. In view of the discussions and findings referred to above I am constrained to hold such a view that the Rule have got much merit to succeed.

20. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 30-9-2015 passed by the learned District Judge, Barisal, in Miscellaneous Appeal No.64 of 2015 rejecting the appeal at the admission hearing upon affirming the judgment and order dated 1-9-2015 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Gouranadi, Barisal in Miscellaneous Case No.25 of 2012 is hereby set aside.

Send down the lower court's record and communicate the judgment and order at once.

End.
