During cross-examination OPW 1 in a reply to a question from the side of the pre-emptors testified that there has been a kabala deed in respect of the disputed property which was duly registered, but the Ekrarnama was not registered. OPW 1 in his testimony conceded that, prior to purchase no notice was served. OPW 2 Anjira Aktar deposed on behalf of the vendor-opposite party Nos. 1 & 2. This witness in her deposition testified that the case land belonged to their father and her father gifted the property in favour of 4 (four) sisters on 18-8-1996. OPW 2 at a stage of her testimony also testified that the case deed is not 'sub kabala', rather; it is a 'mortgage kabala'. OPW 2 denied that the pre-emptors knew about the case kabala for the 1st time on 18-7-1996 from the settlement officials. OPW 3 SM Nazrul Islam in his testimony testified that the case land was mortgaged in favour of Ruhul Amin and on the date of mortgage an Ekrarnama was executed by Ruhul Amin. During cross-examination in a reply to a question from the side of the pre-emptors, OPW 3 frankly admitted that the deed is not at all a mortgage deed, and the case land has been transferred by "kot kabala ekbari".

14. On perusal of the case records it transpires that the learned trial court in the impugned judgment and order with regard to the matter of determination which were five in numbers, decided all the points in favour of the pre-emptors analyzing the evidence on records in its true perspective. It has been conclusively held on assessment of evidence that the case as instituted is maintainable and the pre-emptors have locus standi to institute the original case for pre-emption. With regard to defect of parties no defect is noticed and scrutinizing the pleadings of the parties no where it is found that any necessary party is left out. Furthermore; the pre-emptors during trial prayed for reply of the interrogaiories, but the opposite parties did not furnish any particulars in the form of reply to interrogatories, and, as such, the court below rightly decided the point in favour of the pre-emptors. With regard to the point of limitation and in nature of transfer deed, it is apparent from the face of the document that the deed in question is out and out a sub-kabala deed. Within the recital of the deed, there is no mention about the so-called mortgage or as to the existence of the alleged Ekrarnama. Which will get priority. The evidence on record goes to show that admittedly no notice of transfer was given prior to the transfer deed and the cause of action as cited from the side of the pre-emptors has been corroborated by tangible evidence as adduced from their side. Besides this, with regard to the date of knowledge, from the cross-examination of the witnesses no such discrepancy or material contradiction is noticed by dint of which it can be held that prior to the date of knowledge mentioned, the pre-emptor-respondents were in the know about .the case transfer.

<u>15. Having gone through the connected papers I find that under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 the instant case was filed. Therefore, obviously on the pertinent point in hand as to the opening of a separate mutation khatian as admitted from the side of the pre-emptors and the submission advanced from the side of the learned Counsel Mr Mainuddin on behalf of the pre-emptee-appellant that the pre-emptors are ceased to be a co-sharer by purchase in the case land, it is noticed on careful scrutiny over the relevant papers and apprising the provisions of law provided in section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, that there lies cogent reason to inclined such a view that in a case for pre-emption filed under section 24 of this Act, if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be treated a co-sharer in the entire plot, even if; the land to that plot is recorded in more than one khatian, and in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian, a co-sharer tenant can file a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. Moreover, under the said provision of law the words 'one or more co-sharer tenants of such land' occurring in section 24 of the Act means a co-sharer in the plot, not the holding as mentioned in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 IRef. SM Basiruddin vs Islam, 35 DLR (AD) 230].</u>

16. In the context, I may not be out of place to reproduce the case law referred to by Mr Siddique in the case of Aminullah (Md) vs Serajul Hug, 65 DLR (AD) 82 wherein their Lordships held:

"In a case of pre-emption filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be treated as co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. Therefore, in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian a co-sharer tenant can file a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. The words " one or more co-sharer tenants of such land" occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act means a co-sharer in the plot not the holding as mentioned in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Such being the position of law, the pre-emptors were not even required to file an application for amendment to show that they have also interest in RS Khatian No. 3838. In the case of SM Basiruddin vs Z Islam, 35 DLR (AD) 230, it has been held that the expression 'non-agricultural land' used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used the "Bengal Tenancy Act or State Acquisition of Tenancy Act".

17. Relying upon the aforesaid decisions as well as proposition of law and the facts and circumstances of this case, it appears that the grounds of this appeal are not acceptable.

18. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and the discussions referred to above, I find support in the submission advanced from side of the learned Senior Counsel Mr M Qumrul Haque Siddique, and, as such, I am constrained to hold such a view that in deciding the fate of the original case the learned the then Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna committed no illegality or infirmity by dint of which the impugned judgment and order can be interfered with.

19. In the result; the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

20. Communicate the judgment and order at once.

Send down the Lower Court's Records immediately.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal Nos. 2203-2204 of 2018
lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate instructed by Haridas Paul, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner (In both the cases). 

AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate instructed by Mominuddin, Advocate-on-Record—For the Respondent (In both the cases).
parties:
Rabiul Islam (Md)….. Petitioner (In both the cases)
vs
Asadul Haque (Md) and others...…. Respondents (In both the cases)
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20-3-2018 & 21-3-2018 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 376 of 2017 with 103 of 2017).
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique J: These two petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the common judgment and order dated 20th and 21st March 2018 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos. 103 and 376 of 2017 making both the Rules absolute and remanding the Election Case No.4 of 2006 to the Tribunal with observations and directions.

2. Short facts, for the disposal of these two petitions, are that the leave petitioner Rabiul Islam, instituted aforesaid Election Case before the Election Tribunal, Rajshahi for declaration that the election held on 30-12-2015 in the post of Mayer of Puthia Municipality, Rajshahi was void and for further declaration that the election of Md Asadul Haque as Mayor of said. Municipality was, also void. The respondent No. 1 contested the said election petition. The Tribunal, recording the evidence and considering the materials on record, allowed the election case and declared the election of Mayor of Puthia Municipality, Rajshahi void and also declared that the present petitioner is elected Mayor of the said Municipality.

3. Against the said judgment and order of the Election Tribunal dated 24-11-2016, the respondent No.1 preferred Election Appeal No.2 of 2016 before the Election Appellate Tribunal, Rajshahi. In the Appellate Tribunal, the respondent No.1 filed an application for examining the returning officer and for a direction to the authority concerned to produce the ballot papers of Nos.3, 5 and 6 polling centres. The Election Appellate Tribunal by its order No. 3 dated 23-1-2017 rejected the said prayer. Against which, the respondent No.1 filed Civil Revision No.103 of 2017 in the High Court Division.

4. Thereafter, the Election Appellate Tribunal heard the parties and dismissed the election appeal by a judgment and order dated 13-2-2017. Against which, the respondent No.1 filed a civil revisional application in the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order, made both the Rules absolute. Thus, the election petitioner has filed these two separate civil petitions for leave to appeal.

5. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Counsel appearing for petitioner in both the petitions, submits that the instant revisional applications were not at all maintainable since Election Appellate Tribunal is not a court, the High Court Division erred in making the Rules absolute.

6. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent No.1, submits that since the District Judge, Rajshahi heard the appeal so instant revisions were very much maintainable. In his submissions he supported the judgment and order of the High Court Division.

7. The moot question is, "are Election Tribunals and Election Appellate Tribunals Courts for the purpose of section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure." In other words, against the judgment and order of the Election Appellate Tribunal civil revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable or not.

8. It appears from the materials produced in this Division that Election Commission constituted the Election Tribunal and Election Appellate Tribunal exercising its power vested under section 24 of Local Government (Pourashava) Ain 2009. The relevant notification of Constitution of the Election Tribunals and Election Appellate Tribunals runs as follows:

“নির্বাচন কমিশন

বাংলাদেশ

নির্বাচন কমিশন সচিবালয়

শেরেবাংলা নগর, ঢাকা

www.ecs.gov.bd

আইন – 1

শাখা নং-১৭.০০.০০০০.০৪৫.৬২.০০৯.১৫.০৮

তারিখঃ ২৪ জানুয়ারি ২০১৬ খ্রিঃ

বিষয়ঃ নির্বাচন ট্রাইব্যুনাল ও নির্বাচন আপিল ট্রাইব্যুনাল গঠন সংক্রান্ত গেজেট ।

উপযুক্ত বিষয়ে আদিষ্ট হয়ে ৬৪ টি জেলাসমূহের আওতাভুক্ত সকল পৌরসভার মেয়র, সংরক্ষিত আসনের কাউন্সিলর ও সাধারন আসনের কাউন্সিলর পদে নির্বাচনী বিরোধ সংক্রান্ত দায়েরকৃত নির্বাচনী দরখাস্ত ও আপিল গ্রহণ, শুনানি ও নিষ্পত্তির লক্ষ্যে যথাক্রমে নির্বাচন ট্রাইব্যুনালঃ ও নির্বাচন আপিল ট্রাইব্যুনালঃ গঠন সংক্রান্ত গেজেট প্রয়োজনীয় কার্যার্থে এতদসঙ্গে প্রেরণ করা হল।

লায়লা শারমিন

সিনিয়র সহকারী সচিব (আইন – 1)

ফোনঃ৯১৮-০৭০৩”

9. The decision for Constitution of Election Tribunals and Election Appellate Tribunals was published, at the instance of the Election Commission, in the Bangladesh Gazette on 7-1-2016. The relevant provision of section 24 of the Local Government (Pourashava) Ain 2009 regarding the authority of Election Commission to constitute such Election Tribunals and Election Appellate Tribunals runs us follows: —

“২৪। নির্বাচন ট্রাইব্যুনাল ও নির্বাচন আপিল ট্রাইবুনাল গঠন।– (১) এই আইনের অধীন নির্বাচন সম্পর্কিত বিরোধ নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে নির্বাচন কমিশন একজন উপযুক্ত পদমর্যাদার বিচারবিভাগীয় কর্মকর্তার সমন্বয়ে প্রয়োজনীয় সংখ্যক নির্বাচন ট্রাইব্যুনাল এবং একজন উপযুক্ত পদমর্যাদার বিচারবিভাগীয় কর্মকর্তার সমন্বয়ে প্রয়োজনীয় সংখ্যক নির্বাচন আপীল ট্রাইব্যুনাল গঠন করিবে।”

10. That is, law provides that the Election Commission shall constitute Election Appellate Tribunal by "একজন উপযুক্ত পদমর্যাদার বিচারবিভাগীয় কর্মকর্তার সমন্বয়ে " Section 24 (4) provides that, " নির্বাচন আপিল ট্রাইব্যুনালের রায় চূড়ান্ত বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে ।" Special provisions as to filing Election Petition, procedure for filing election petition, jurisdiction of election Tribunals and Election Appellate Tribunals and the procedures for holding trial to be followed by the Tribunals, and Appellate Tribunals have been provided in Rules 55, 58, 60 and 61 of the Local Government (Pourashava) Election Rules, 2010. All those are special provisions for adjudicating the election disputes.

<u>11. The differences between courts and tribunals, constituted under the Special Law, and their composition and formation are distinct and separate. Though both of them have similar functions to perform as the tribunals are clothed with trappings of the Courts. All the Courts are tribunal but all the tribunals are not courts. A ‘court’ in the technical sense is a Tribunal constituted by the state as a part of ordinary hierarchy of Courts which are invested with the state's judicial powers. On the other hand, the tribunals are constituted under Special Laws to exercise special jurisdiction in order to decide certain controversy arising under the special Laws. The powers of the tribunal are limited. The Tribunal, as distinguished from the Court, exercises judicial power and decides matter brought before it judicially or quashi-judicially, but it does not constitute a court. The word 'Tribunal' has not been defined in the Constitution. On the other hand, as per provision of Article 152 of the Constitution 'Court' means any Court of law including Supreme Court. To be a Court, it must be entrusted with judicial functions, that is, of deciding litigated questions according to law. On the other hand, the basic test of a tribunal is that it is an adjudicating authority other than a Court vested with the judicial powers. Court referred to in 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure is a regular Civil Court as contemplated in section 3 and 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The jurisdiction, which has been given to the Tribunal to exercise in the capacity of Tribunal and not a regular civil Courts. Even if the Tribunals are presided over by the Judges of regular Courts and exercising the judicial power and discharging judicial functions, that does not make any difference as they still remain as Tribunals only. The Election Appellate Tribunals and Election Tribunals are not Court and they specially constituted as Tribunals for adjudication of the election disputes by an special statute, namely, the Local Government (Pourashava) Ain, 2009.</u>

<u>12. Section 115 of CPC empowers the High Court Division to call for the record of any suit or proceeding in which a decree or an order has been passed by a Court of District Judge or Additional District Judge, or a decree has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge, from which no appeal lies. Apart from other limitations placed upon the exercise of that power, one of the essential requirements for the High Court Division to exercise its revisional jurisdiction is that the order sought to be revised must have been made by the aforementioned Courts subordinate to the High Court Division. The Tribunals are meant to deal with only specific class of cases. They do not and cannot exercise powers vested, in a civil court for decision of civil disputes in general within the meaning of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Such Tribunals cannot therefore be termed as Civil Courts within the meaning of sections 3, 9 and 115 of the Code.</u>

<u>13. The High Court division has committed an error of law in not construing the sprit of the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 172 (AKM Ruhul Amin vs District Judge). The then Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 provided the provision of preferring appeal in section 29(4) which was that any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the election in dispute was held. But in the present law provision of preferring appeal has been provided to the " নির্বাচন আপিল ট্রাইব্যুনাল ", which has been constituted not by the District Judge but by " একজন উপযুক্ত পদমর্যাদার বিচারবিভাগীয় কর্মকর্তার সমন্বয়ে ". The question arose in the cited case was whether the District Judge in passing the impugned order, was exercising powers of a Court or acting as a persona designata. It was observed by this Division that District Judge acted not a persona designata but a court subordinate to the High Court Division.</u>

<u>14. Since the Election Appellate Tribunal is not a court, we are of the view that the High Court Division committed error of law in entertaining the revisional applications exercising its revisional, jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

<u>Accordingly, both the petitions are disposed of. The judgment and order of the High Court Division are hereby set aside.</u>

End.

lawyer:
M Qumrul Haque Siddiqi, Senior Advocate with Tanvir Parvez, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 

Md Khurshid Alam Khan with Zainul Abedin and Faria Huq, Advocates—For the Respondents.
parties:
Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto) ......... Petitioner
VS
1. Rokeya Din, 2. Aysha Huq, 3. Afzal Husain Choudhury, 4. Zahed Chowdhury and others ...... Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: By filing an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 (hereinafter referred to as the Arbitration Act), the petitioner challenges the legality and propriety of (i) formation of the arbitral tribunal comprising the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 5, (ii) the performance of the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators and (iii) the interim Order passed by the aforesaid arbitral tribunal on 2-8-2018.

2. In the application, it is averred that the petitioner is the partner of a partnership concern, named, Metro Super Centre (hereinafter referred to as the MSC) which is comprised of 2 (two) partners, namely, the petitioner and the respondent No. 4. The MSC was created through a Deed of Partnership dated 1-9-2012, which was registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) on 2-10-2012. It is stated that in the course of running the aforesaid partnership business, when disagreements among the partners surfaced to a great extent, the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 decided to amicably settle the dispute through mediation and, for that purpose, they appointed respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the mediators, who happen to be close relatives of both the parties. On 12-3-2018 the mediators laid down certain conditions to be observed by the partners, including a direction upon the partners to conduct an audit to be carried out by a Chartered Accountant Firm (CA firm) named, Hoda Vasi Chowdhury & Company. However, without any reason, the mediators started to act as arbitrators and, eventually, on an application filed by the respondent No. 4, the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 passed an interim Order on 2-8-2018 authorizing the respondent No.5 (CEO and the Manager of the MSC) to jointly operate the bank account of the MSC. Thereafter, the respondent No. 4 approached the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka for execution of the aforesaid interim Order dated 2-8-2018 by filing the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 under section 21(4) of the Arbitration Act. After admission of the above Arbitration Miscellaneous Case on 12-8-2018, the learned District Judge, Dhaka directed to run the business of the MSC as per the arbitral tribunal's interim Order dated 2-8-2018 till 23-10-2018. Thereafter, the petitioner having appeared before the Court on 19-8-2018 filed an application under section 7A(5) of the Arbitration Act for rejection of the aforesaid Arbitration Miscellaneous Case. The learned District Judge fixed the matter on 5-9-2018 for hearing the petitioner, but the petitioner opted to approach this Court and filed the instant arbitration application.

3. By filing an affidavit-in-opposition, the respondent No. 4 states that the petitioner deliberately distorted the true accounts of the facts of this case, for, the petitioner unequivocally agreed through e-mails dated 7-2-2018 and 8-2-2018 to appoint the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators for settlement of the dispute between them and, also, gave his undertaking to accept and abide by the decisions oaf the arbitrators. The respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 were never nominated as the mediators, rather the arbitrators first tried for an amicable settlement otherwise than pursuing arbitration proceedings and pursuant to the failure of the settlement between the parties, the arbitrators started arbitration process based on certain terms and conditions as stipulated and agreed upon by the parties vide arbitration agreement dated 12-3-2018. The arbitrators ordered for audit of the MSC to be carried out by an independent auditor, named, Hoda Vasi Chowdhury & Co. It is claimed that the CA Firm was though selected by the arbitrators, but was appointed upon obtaining approval from the petitioner vide e-mail 14-7-2018. In clause 9 of the arbitration agreement executed under the heading/title 'The Decisions of the Arbitrators/Mediators' (biggo moddhostotakarider siddhanto), it was clearly stipulated that based on the audit report, the arbitrators would give their decisions which would be binding on both the parties. It is alleged that the petitioner was in the management and control of the MSC and did not co-operate with the auditor which has been reflected in the audit report. It is stated that the petitioner, subsequent to receipt of the audit report, although has acknowledged the audit report from the auditors and the 'arbitrators', however, after perusing the said audit report, which accounted for his misdeeds in the business, challenged the role of the arbitrators by creating a false claim that the arbitrators were appointed as mediators, not as arbitrators.

4. It is stated that pursuant to filing the present application, the High Court Division on 3-9-2018 passed Stay Order upon the interim Order dated 2-8-2018 passed by the arbitrators and, thereafter, the petitioner filed a criminal case, being Tejgaon Thana Case No. 20 dated 5-9-2018 under sections 381/114/109 of the Penal Code, 1860, against the respondent Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5. The background fact of filing the above-mentioned criminal case and its subsequent events are stated to be as follows: that the petitioner while running the management of the MSC opened an L/C for importing goods in the name of the MSC and the said imported goods were lying at the Chittagong Port having been marked for auction, and since the petitioner was removed and replaced by Mr Navid Chowdhury (respondent No. 5) as the CEO vide the interim Order passed by the arbitral tribunal, Mr Navid Chowdhury got the imported goods released from the Chittagong Port and on 29-8-2018 brought the goods to Dhaka and stored in the godown of the MSC. It is stated that at the time of admission of the instant arbitration application, this Court directed the petitioner not to use 66 (sixty six) signed-cheques given by the respondent No. 4 including other signed cheque, if any, held by the petitioner and, also, directed to return the same to the respondent No. 4 within 7 (seven) days, from the date of receipt of the Order and to file an affidavit-in-compliance about the return of these aforesaid cheques within 2 (two) weeks thereafter; that the respondent No. 4 after obtaining the bail from the Court of competent jurisdiction filed the Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 50198 of 2018 before this Court for quashing the above-mentioned criminal case (GR No. 392 of 1918 arising out of Tejgaon Thana Case No. 20 dated 5-9-2018 under sections 381/114/109 of the Penal Code, pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka; that a Division Bench of this Court after hearing the parties issued a Rule and stayed all further proceedings of the above-mentioned criminal case for a period of 3 (three) months on 31-10-2018 so far as it relates to respondent No. 4; that the said Rule is now pending for hearing before this Court.

5. Mr Tanvir Parvez, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3, upon misconception of law, have considered themselves as the arbitrators and have most illegally exercised the powers which are meant exclusively for the arbitrators in the Arbitration Act and, as such, the impugned interim Order should be declared to be without lawful authority. He submits that the opposite parties have failed to consider that they have not been appointed as the arbitrators under clause 20 of the Partnership Deed and, therefore, they have no power to pass interim Order. In an endeavour to place the above count of submissions in greater details, he submits that the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 have failed to consider that there is a fundamental difference between mediation and arbitration inasmuch as, while the provisions of the Arbitration Act applies in case of arbitration, the same have no application in a case of mediation. He argues that in view of the above position of law, their action as arbitrators and passing the interim Order is outside their jurisdiction and, as such, it should be declared without lawful authority. He takes this Court through the provisions of section 12 of the Arbitration Act, and submits that the law sets out specific procedures for appointing arbitrators, but it is evident in this case that the said procedures were not followed in appointing the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 which conclusively indicate that it was never the intention of the parties to appoint the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators, rather they were appointed as the mediators and, as such, there being no existence of arbitral tribunal, the impugned interim Order should be declared without any lawful authority.

6. By making the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays to declare that the actions of the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators are without lawful authority and the Order dated 2-8-2018 passed by the aforesaid persons purportedly claiming themselves to be the members of the arbitral tribunal is illegal.

7. Ms Faria Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4, takes me through clause 20 of the Deed of Partnership and submits that it is clear as the day-light that the respondent No. 4 has invoked the aforesaid arbitration clause. In elaborating her above count of submissions, she submits that the provisions of clause 20 of the Deed of Partnership and the e-mail correspondences between the petitioner and his partner related to the nomination and formation of arbitration team were all written in English where the term 'arbitrator' has been used at all the times and the term "mediator" was never used for a single time whatsoever in any form. Then Ms. Huq places the provisions of section 6 of the Arbitration Act in tandem with referring the case of Joinal Abedin Jamal vs Noor Afzal, 63 DLR 432, and submits that, without prejudice to the other submissions, if it is presumed that the arbitration clause has not been invoked by the respondent No. 4, the petitioner, vide section 6 of the Arbitration Act, has waived his right to object as he has proceeded with the arbitration without stating his objection to such noncompliance of invoking the arbitration clause without undue delay. Ms. Huq next places before this Court the arbitration agreement dated 12-3-2018 executed by the petitioner and his partner, and submits that it was prepared in consultation with all the parties with mutually agreed terms and conditions and was properly executed on a non-judicial stamp and, by its clause 9, the arbitrators were authorized to award decisions binding upon both the parties. By taking this Court through section 17(a) and (b) of the Arbitration Act, she submits that since the arbitral tribunal comprising the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 is legally empowered to rule on its own jurisdiction on whether there is existence of a valid arbitration agreement or not and, also, whether the arbitral tribunal was properly constituted or not, the petitioner ought to have approached the arbitral tribunal, at first. She argues that the petitioner has come to the wrong forum to challenge the validity of the agreement dated 12-3-2018 as it falls under the purview of the decision of the arbitral tribunal. By placing the provisions of section 22 of the Arbitration Act, Ms. Huq submits that the petitioner is deliberately trying to confuse this Court with regard to the terms 'mediators' and 'arbitrators' inasmuch as the law mandates the arbitrators to play the role of mediators for an amicable settlement and, accordingly, the arbitrators initially approached as the mediators to settle the dispute amicably. She continues to submit that there is no fundamental distinction between the terminologies 'mediator' and 'arbitrator' if the same are translated into Bengali, because as per the Dictionary published by the Bangla Academy, the meaning of both the words 'mediation' and 'arbitration' is "মধ্যস্থতা". Ms. Huq agitates that the agreement dated 12-3-2018 under the title "The Decision of the Arbitrators/Mediators" (বিজ্ঞ মধ্যস্থতাকারীদের সিদ্ধান্ত) is being simply misinterpreted by the petitioner to mislead the Court with malafide intention to cause obstacles in the arbitration proceedings and to cause financial loss to the respondent No. 4. By placing the provisions of section 20(2)(a) of the Arbitration Act, Ms. Faria Huq submits that in view of the fact that the learned District Judge had to adjourn the hearing of the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 resulting in substantial loss in cost, instead of saving the expenses of the parties, the petitioner's approach before this Court, thus, is contrary to the provision of section 20(2)(a) of the Arbitration Act.

8. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the respondents prays for discharging the Rule with exemplary costs.

9. Given the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, this Court considered it useful to call the parties to the arbitral proceedings as well as all the three arbitrators before this Court with an aim to have first-hand information about the background and all other events from them, so that this case can be disposed of more effectively and fairly. Accordingly, they all appeared before this Court in person and narrated the facts in their own style.

10. After hearing all of them, it revealed that the partners of the MSC (the petitioner and the respondent No. 4) are full brothers and they are the sons of late Obaidul Huq Chowdhury who is the founding editor of Dhaka Law Reports (DLR). Also, the members of the arbitral tribunal are their close relatives (the Chairman of the arbitral tribunal is a cousin, one member, namely, Mrs. Aysha Huq is a full sister, and another member, namely, Mrs. Rokeya Din is a niece of the partners of the MSC). This Court eventually told all of them in the open Court that since it has come to the knowledge of this Court that the partners of the MSC are the sons of such a late lamented person to whom the judiciary of Bangladesh is indebted for his contribution in law reporting of this country, which he undertook immediately after establishment of the Dhaka High Court, by which the Judges and the lawyers of this country are being greatly benefited, this Court, therefore, instead of letting this matter to be dragged on for long, wishes to resolve the dispute between the parties amicably and, accordingly, asked them to sit together and put in their best efforts to find out a solution. It was opined by this Court that the criminal case filed by the petitioner in connection with this matter appears to this Court to be very unusual inasmuch as, the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 being the partners of the MSC are the joint owners of the goods, which are alleged to have been stolen by a partner, namely, respondent No. 4, and there is no scope to record a criminal case against a person on the allegation of stealing of the goods which belonged to him. It was also commented by this Court that in the case MH Khondker vs AW Qazilbash, 20 DLR 945, this Court has laid down a ratio that during pendency of any suit/case, if any party seeks to create pressure upon the other side, it amounts to interference with the course of justice. This Court made the observation that since the dispute among them is with regard to the business owned jointly by them and the District Judge's Court of Dhaka and this Court were in seisin of this matter, filing of criminal case alleging removal/stealing goods of the said business amounts to committing contempt of Court. This Court has taken judicial notice of the fact that the criminal case was filed immediately after obtaining the Order of stay from this Court on the operation of the Order passed by the learned District Judge enforcing the arbitral tribunal's interim Order dated 2-8-2018. When this Court asked the petitioner of the instant application, Mr Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto), about the filing of the criminal case, in reply thereto, he told that in fact he did not have any intention to file the criminal case; he only wanted to lodge a General Diary (GD). All the three arbitrators contended that as the senior family members, all that they want to see that these petitioners' business is saved and, with this aim, they were trying their best to resolve the dispute without causing further damage not only to the business, but also to their personal and family relationship. In reply to a query made by this Court as to whether it would be possible for them to continue with their duties as the arbitrators, they informed this Court that they would be happy to resign for the sake of an acceptable resolution of the dispute. Finally, while the arbitrators opted to leave the matter upon this Court for finding a better solution even at the cost of reconstituting the tribunal either replacing them all or keeping anyone whom the Court considers to be useful, serviceable and acceptable, the learned Advocates of the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 insisted upon this Court that they expect a verdict from this Court as to the legality of the formation of the arbitral tribunal and the validity of the impugned interim Order. Under the circumstances, this Court decided to proceed with the hearing which culminated into delivering of the instant full-fledged Judgment.

11. Upon hearing the learned Advocates for both the sides, on perusal of the petitioner's application as well as the affidavits filed by the respondents together with their annexures and having read the relevant statutory laws and case-laws cited from the various Law Journals, it appears to this Court that the following issues are to be adjudicated upon by this Court; (i) whether there is existence of any arbitration agreement between the partners of the MSC i.e. between the present petitioner and the respondent No. 4, (ii) whether the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 were appointed as the arbitrators or as the mediators, and whether the arbitral tribunal was formed as per the provisions of law, (iii) whether the arbitral tribunal was competent to pass the impugned interim Order, whether the interim Order was a proper and legal one, and whether the interim Order passed by the arbitral tribunal can be challenged before the High Court Division, (iv) whether the law permits the petitioner to challenge the legality and propriety of formation of the arbitration tribunal comprising the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and, thereby, to question the performance of the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators, (v) whether the petitioner is competent to file the instant application during pendency of the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case before the Court of District Judge, (vi) whether this Court is competent to entertain and adjudicate upon the question relating to jurisdiction of the arbitration tribunal, (vii) whether the petitioner has waived his right to challenge the appointment of the arbitrators and to object to the impugned interim Order, (viii) whether the present Members and the Chairman of arbitral tribunal should continue to perform their functions, (ix) whether this Court should constitute/create a new arbitral tribunal and (x) whether the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 pending before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka should be kept in abeyance, so that the new arbitrators may review the impugned interim Order passed by the arbitration tribunal on 2-8-2018.

12. Let me take up the first issue, namely, whether there is existence of any arbitration agreement between the partners of the MSC i.e. between the present petitioner and the respondent No. 4. Upon skimming through the Deed of Partnership dated 1-9-2012 executed by the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 on 1-9-2012, it transpires that clause 20 of the Partnership Deed contains a provision of arbitration in the following terms:

"That in case of a difference of opinion among the partners with regard to the constitution, meaning and effect of this Deed of Partnership in respect of the accounts or dissolution or any other matter relating to running the partnership firm shall be decided upon by two (2) arbitrators nominated by the partners and legal representatives of the partners or and in case of difference of any opinion among them the matter will be decided upon by an umpire selected by the arbitrators".

13. Thus, it is an admitted position that in the event of any disagreement between the partners, they may seek to resolve the dispute through arbitration. Now, the question that crops up for consideration as to whether the arbitral tribunal was constituted as per the terms of the clause 20 of the Partnership Deed and, also, in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration Act.

<u>14. Section 11(1) of the Arbitration Act states that the parties shall be at liberty to determine the number of arbitrators and, as per the provisions of section 11(3) of the Arbitration Act, if the parties appoint an even number of arbitrators, a Chairman shall be appointed by the arbitrators. From a careful reading of clause 20 of the Partnership deed, it appears to this Court that the petitioner and the respondent No. 4 have agreed to form a three-member arbitral tribunal through appointing one arbitrator by each of the party and, then, the two arbitrators shall appoint the Chairman.</u>

15. In this case, from the e-mail sent by the respondent No. 4 to the petitioner on 7-2-2018 at 5-52 pm, as evident from annexure X-1, it transpires that the respondent No. 4 initially proposed the name of Mr Muzammel Huq Babu as his arbitrator and, in replying to the above e-mail, the petitioner wrote to the respondent No. 4 on 8-2-2018 at 4-21 pm that his arbitrator will be Mr Debhorta Laha, as evident from annexure X-2. From the e-mail sent by the petitioner on 28-2-2018 at 8-45 pm to Mr Afzal Husain Choudhury (respondent No. 3), it appears that the petitioner undertook to accept the verdict of the arbitration tribunal. From annexure X-6, it transpires that the respondent No. 4 appointed Mrs. Rokeya Din (respondent No. 1) in place of his initially nominated arbitrator Mr Muzammel Huq Babu about whom the petitioner raised objection. It further transpires that on receipt of the audit report by the petitioner, he sent an e-mail on 14-7-2018 at 02-46 pm to Mr Afzal Choudhury (respondent No. 3) in the following terms "thank you for providing a copy of reports from auditors and arbitrator. In reference to the Arbitration Agreement dated March 12, 2018 the auditor report is an absolute requirement.........I still hope that you the arbitrators will find a fair resolution", as evident from annexure-X5. Thus, from the above discussed e-mail correspondences, of which the latest one is dated 14-7-2018 being a couple of weeks before the impugned interim Order dated 2-8-2018, it surfaces that the petitioner, after appointing the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3, has been addressing them as the arbitrators all along, that is to say, from the commencement of the arbitration in the early part of February, 2018 till passing the interim Order by the arbitrators on 2-8-2018. Beside the above-mentioned correspondences, I have read all the e-mail correspondences made by the petitioner with Mr Afzal Husain Choudhury, wherefrom it transpires that the respondent Nos. 1, 2, and 3 were nominated and appointed as the arbitrators as per the terms of clause No. 20 of the Partnership Deed dated 1-9-2012 and all the correspondences mentioned them as the arbitrators from the beginning of their assignment.

16. Now, let me see on what basis the petitioner seeks to make out a case that the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 have not been appointed as the arbitrators; they have been appointed as the mediators. Upon hearing the learned Advocate and examining the annexures appended to the instant petition, it transpires that the petitioner's basis of such claim is the written agreement dated 12-3-2018 executed between the partners of the MSC (the petitioner and the respondent No. 4) and all the three arbitrators, which was witnessed by two witnesses, namely, the wife of the petitioner and another person, who happens to be the common brother-in-law of the petitioner and the respondent No. 4. And, the reason for terming the arbitrators as the mediators is that the document (agreement dated 12-3-2018) incorporates the Bengali word  ‘মধ্যস্থতাকারী’. However, it is evident from the correspondences that the arbitration proceedings commenced in the first week of February, 2018 and, in course of the arbitration proceedings, the arbitrators took a step to mediate the dispute in the month of March 2018 in an effort to resolve the dispute expeditiously and more effectively. Since the arbitrators are the close relatives of the petitioner as well as the respondent No. 4, the arbitrators' above step appears to this Court to be bonafide and is also very much within the provisions of law, inasmuch as section 22 of the Arbitration Act allows the arbitrators to opt for such a path. section 22 of the Arbitration Act states that—"it shall not be incompatible with an arbitration agreement for an arbitral tribunal to encourage settlement of the dispute otherwise than by arbitration and, with the agreement of all the parties, the arbitral tribunal may use mediation, conciliation or any other procedures at any time during the arbitral proceedings to encourage settlement."

<u>17. More importantly, the agreement dated 12-3-2018 is written in Bengali and if the word ‘মধ্যস্থতাকারী’is translated from the Bengali to English, the Dictionary published by the Bangla Academy provides the meaning of the word `11143wilsit' as both 'arbitrator' or 'mediator'. That is to say that if the entire document is translated into English, the word in question would have to be read as 'arbitrator'. Moreover, the fundamental difference between the mediators and the arbitrators are on the question of authority with powers related to giving a binding decision or not. And, since in clause 9 of the aforesaid arbitration agreement dated 12-3-2018 the arbitrators were authorized to award decisions binding upon both the parties, the agreement has the binding force upon the parties and, therefore, the agreement dated 12-3-2018 should be seen as a piece of document related to arbitration. Thus, this Court finds that the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 were never appointed as the mediators and they, having been appointed as the arbitrators, have constituted a lawful arbitral tribunal.</u>

<u>18. Let me now take up the issue No. 3, namely, whether the arbitral tribunal was competent to pass the impugned interim Order, whether the interim Order was a proper and legal one and whether the impugned Order is appealable/ challengeable in this Court. In view of the findings of this Court that the arbitral tribunal was formed as per the terms of the Partnership Deed dated 1-9-2012 and, also, in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration Act, this Court has no option but to hold that the arbitral tribunal was well competent to pass any interim Order as mandated by the provisions of section 21 of the Arbitration Act. Since the proviso to sub-section (3) of section 21 of the Arbitration Act empowers the arbitral tribunal to pass an ex-parte interim Order in an appropriate case to meet the exigency, I find the impugned interim Order to be proper and legal. Although the interim Order in question has been signed by two arbitrators namely, Mrs Aysha Huq and Mr Afzal Husain Choudhury, but it cannot be termed as an irregular Order, let alone to be an illegal Order. Because, after constitution of an arbitral tribunal, it may proceed to function with only two arbitrators, unless the third arbitrator raises any objection to any step taken or Order passed by the two arbitrators. Since, the third arbitrator, Mrs Rokeya Din, has not raised any objection to the interim Order in question, the same is to be taken as a valid and lawful Order of a properly constituted arbitral tribunal. And, in view of the clear stipulations made in section 21(1) of the Arbitration Act that no appeal shall lie against any interim Order passed by the arbitral tribunal, an aggrieved party neither can approach this Court directly, nor the propriety and legality of an interim Order passed by the arbitral tribunal can be challenged in the form of seeking a declaration from a civil Court of first instance because of the prohibition imposed by the Legislature in section 7 of the Arbitration Act.</u>

19. I would now take up the fourth issue, namely, whether the law permits the petitioner to challenge the legality and propriety of formation of the arbitration tribunal comprising the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and, thereby, to question the performance of the respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as the arbitrators. For adjudication upon the above issue, it appears to me that since the petitioner has questioned the appointment and performance of the arbitrators, quotation of the relevant portions of sections 13 and 14 of the Arbitration Act would be useful.

13. Grounds for challenge—

(1)   ...............

(2)   ..............

(3) An arbitrator may be challenged only if circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his independence or impartiality, or he does not possess the qualifications agreed to by the parties.

(4)   ..............

14. Challenge procedure—

(1)   ............

(2) Failing any agreement referred to in sub-section (1), a party who intends to challenge an arbitrator shall, within thirty days after becoming aware of the circumstances referred to in sub-section (3) of section 13, send a written statement of the reasons for the challenge to the arbitral tribunal.

(3) Unless the arbitrator challenged under sub-section (2), withdraws from his office or the other party agrees to the challenge, the arbitral tribunal shall decide on the challenge within thirty days from the date of filing the written statement referred to in sub-section 2.

(4) Any party aggrieved by the decision of the arbitral tribunal under sub-section (3), may prefer an appeal to the High Court Division within thirty days from the date of the said decision.

(5)   ..............

(6)   .............

<u>20. From the above provisions of law, it appears that a party to an arbitration agreement may challenge any arbitrator's competency and impartiality by making a written representation to the arbitral tribunal within 30 (thirty) days of knowing about the incompetency or partiality of the concerned arbitrator.</u>

<u>21. In this case, the impugned interim Order was passed on 2-8-2018, the respondent No. 4 approached the Court of District Judge on 12-8-2018 for enforcement of the said Order and the petitioner entered his appearance on 19-8-2018. So, for the sake of argument, if it is presumed that the petitioner was not aware of appointment of arbitrators and formation of the tribunal and he came to know only after receiving notice from the Court of District Judge, Dhaka pursuant to filing the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 on 12-8-2018, it transpires that the petitioner has still time to approach the arbitral tribunal inasmuch as his thirty days would have expired on 13-9-2018. Since before expiry of thirty days, he approached this Court on 30-8-2018 wrongly, the period spent in this wrong forum shall not be counted and, accordingly, he is competent to approach the tribunal within fourteen days of receipt of this judgment to challenge the appointment of the arbitrators. Thus, this Court holds that the petitioner is at liberty to challenge the appointment and performance/actions of the arbitrators before the arbitral tribunal within the remaining time-limit, and if the arbitrators do not step down from their respective positions, the petitioner shall have the right to prefer an appeal before this Court.</u>

22. And, if the petitioner's intention is to obtain a ruling on the jurisdiction of the tribunal, the petitioner ought to have approached the tribunal. In this regard, this Court finds it useful to look at the provisions of section 17 of the Arbitration Act, which run as follows:

17. Competence of arbitral tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction—Unless other-wise agreed by the parties, the arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction on any questions including the following issues, namely—

(a) whether there is existence of a valid arbitration agreement;

(b) whether the arbitral tribunal is properly constituted;

(c) whether the arbitration agreement is against the public policy.

(d) whether the arbitration agreement is incapable of being performed, and,

(e) what matters have been submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement.

<u>23. From a plain reading of the above provisions, it can be noticed that the Legislature has endowed the arbitral tribunal with the power to adjudicate upon the issue as to its own competency. Therefore, it was incumbent upon the petitioner to ask the tribunal to decide on the question as to whether the tribunal is properly constituted or not. It means that the Arbitration Act permits a party to an arbitration agreement to challenge the competency and impartiality of a single arbitrator or all the arbitrators by filing a written representation to the arbitral tribunal, so that the arbitral tribunal itself can give a decision on the aforesaid application for challenge. Also, if a party to the arbitration agreement raises question that the arbitral tribunal is not properly constituted, it is a mandatory duty of the arbitral tribunal to pass an Order on the issue.</u>

24. Let me now adjudicate upon the fifth issue, namely, whether the petitioner is competent to file the instant application during pendency of the Miscellaneous Arbitration Case before the Court of the District Judge. The above issue has been structured to answer the argument of the learned Advocate for the respondent No.4 that by section 53 of the Arbitration Act, the Legislature intended that whenever any party to an arbitration agreement would approach a Court regarding any issue arising out of the said arbitration agreement, all the subsequent applications have to be filed in the said Court. Therefore, let me be familiar with the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act, which is quoted below:

53. Jurisdiction—Notwithstanding any-thing contained elsewhere in this Act or in another law for the time being in force, where with respect to an arbitration agreement any application under this Act has been made in a Court—

(a) that Court alone shall have jurisdiction over the arbitral proceedings, and

(b) all subsequent applications arising out of that agreement and the arbitral proceedings shall be made in that Court and in no other Court.

<u>25. The literal meaning of the above provisions is that once a party to an arbitration agreement approaches any Court, all the parties to the said arbitration agreement shall have to go to that Court for filing any additional or consequential or ancillary or any independent application, until the arbitral proceedings finally comes to an end.</u>

26. However, from a minute reading of the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act, it appears to this Court that it requires an extensive and in-depth statutory interpretation taking into consideration the following scenario; (a) if a party to the arbitration, at first, approaches the District Judge Court for obtaining interim Order before formation of the arbitral tribunal and, thereafter, if the said party challenges an arbitrator's competency or impartiality to the arbitral tribunal unsuccessfully, in that event, the said aggrieved party requires to prefer an appeal under section 14(4) of the Arbitration Act and the pertinent question then would arise as to whether section 53 of the Arbitration Act is capable of taking away the specific appellate jurisdiction of the High Court Division for the purpose of conferring the said jurisdiction on its subordinate Court, (b) if a party to the arbitration agreement, initially, approaches the District Judge Court for appointment of an arbitrator and, later on, his challenge about the competency and impartiality of an arbitrator before the arbitral tribunal fails, will he approach the District Judge Court ignoring the specific appellate jurisdiction of the High Court Division conferred upon it by section 14(4) of the Arbitration Act, (c) when a foreign party of a civil suit pending in the District Judge Court makes an application for staying the proceedings under section 10 of the Arbitration Act, will the foreign party file application for interim Order in the District Judge Court, in the backdrop of existence of the provisions of section 7A of the Arbitration Act, which requires that the High Court Division shall hear such application, (d) when a party to the arbitration, at first, approaches the District Judge Court either for obtaining interim Order under section 7A of the Arbitration Act or makes application under section 10 of the Arbitration Act in the District Judge Court for staying proceedings of the civil suit pending therein or asks the District Judge Court to appoint the arbitrator under section 12 of the Arbitration Act and, then, during pendency of the arbitral proceeding, if he wants to challenge the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal in a Court, not in the arbitral tribunal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, will the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act be of any use for him to approach the Court of District Judge, in other words, will the jurisdiction and power of the High Court Division under section 20 of the Arbitration Act be ipso facto conferred upon and exercised by the District Judge Court and (e) when a party to the arbitral proceedings approaches the District Judge Court invoking section 21(4) of the Arbitration Act for enforcement of the interim Order, whether any party to the said arbitration is barred from approaching the High Court Division by the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act for making applications under sections 7A, 10, 12 and 20 of the Arbitration Act.

27. There are two vital aspects of the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act. The first aspect is that through its non-obstante provisions, it seeks to herald that irrespective of any statements, stipulations and provisions to the contrary made in the Arbitration Act, or any other law, the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act shall stand. The second aspect is—if any party to the arbitration agreement registers its name in a Court for any purpose, that Court shall assume jurisdiction over the arbitration agreement and arbitral agreement in whose connection a party have moved before the Court.

28. Now, the question comes up for consideration as to whether the jurisdiction conferred specifically upon, and the power vested exclusively in, the High Court Division vide sections 7A, 10, 12, 14(4) and 20 of the Arbitration Act can be discarded by a non-obstante provision, and that too for the purpose of endowing a sub-ordinate Court with the said jurisdiction and power of the High Court Division. While as a normal course of action, the Legislature does not go for enactment of a law by which the superior Court's jurisdiction and power will be scrapped or curtailed in order to enrich and empower the subordinate Courts with the said jurisdiction and power, yet if the Legislature in their wisdom considers it necessary, they are competent to enact such law. However, this sort of enactment is normally made by the Legislature in clearer and specific expressions and, furthermore, in passing such laws the Parliament usually tables some explanations before the House.

<u>29. Given the fact that in section 53 of the Arbitration Act, the Legislature has incorporated the word "কোনো আদালতে" (in a Court), and section 2(b) of the Arbitration Act defines "Court" means "District Judge's Court and includes Additional District Judge's Court appointed by the Government for discharging the functions of District Judge's Court under this Act through Gazette notification", it is difficult for anyone to comprehend the literal meaning. Because, though in ordinary sense the High Court Division is also a Court, but the Legislature consciously has not included the High Court Division as the 'Court' in section 2(b), rather the Parliament has provided a separate definition of the 'High Court Division' in section 2(q) in the following terms; "High Court Division means High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh". Therefore, this Court is led to hold that 'Court' means District Judge Court and, thus, the literal meaning should be that whenever any party to an arbitration agreement will take recourse to the Court of District Judge of any particular District, the said District Judge Court shall have the exclusive jurisdiction over the said arbitration matter up to the period of final termination of the arbitral proceedings, and not any other District Judge Court. The specific jurisdictions conferred upon the High Court Division, thus, are not meant to have been taken away by the provisions of section 53 of the Arbitration Act. The golden rule of statutory interpretation is that when any ambiguity appears in a provision of a statute, the first option for the Court is to find out its literal meaning. And, in the event that it becomes a complex task for the Court to go with the above rule, only then, the Court would endeavour to discover its meaning with the help of the preamble and other provisions of the concerned statute without making any of its provisions nugatory. In this case, if this Court interprets the word "Court" to be the all types of Court, then, while on the one hand, sections 2(b) and 2(q) shall turn to be superfluous, on the other hand, the specific jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court Division will be abridged abruptly.</u>

30. Having held as above, 1 find that since it is beyond the jurisdiction of the Court of District Judge, Dhaka to decide on the issue of the competency, impartiality of the arbitrators and to rule on the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal, the petitioner's apparent fora for that purpose are (i) the arbitral tribunal itself and (ii) the High Court Division.

31. Given the fact that the respondent No. 4 has approached the Court of the District Judge for enforcement of the interim Order passed by the arbitral tribunal under section 21(4) of the Arbitration Act and the said Court being incapable of assuming jurisdiction under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, the petitioner has nothing to agitate before the aforesaid Court.

32. The sixth issue is whether this Court is competent to entertain and adjudicate upon the question relating to jurisdiction of arbitration tribunal. Since the petitioner's apparent fora for addressing his grievances are either the arbitral tribunal to invoke the provisions of sections 14(2) and 17(b) of the Arbitration Act or the High Court Division to invoke section 20 of the Arbitration Act and, seemingly, the petitioner availed himself of the forum of the High Court Division, thus, at this stage, it would be profitable if the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act are examined by the Court. Section 20 of the Arbitration Act runs as follows:

20. Powers of the High Court Division in deciding jurisdiction—(1) The High Court Division may, on the application of any of the parties to the arbitration agreement, after serving notice upon all other parties, determine any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal.

(2) No application under this section shall be taken into account, unless the High Court Division is satisfied that—

(a) The determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs.

(b) the application was submitted without any delay; and

(c) there is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court.

(3) The application shall state—

The reasons on which the matter should be decided by the High Court Division.

(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section, the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award.

<u>33. From a minute reading of the entire provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, my understanding is that sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act is the provision which enables and empowers the High Court Division to entertain an application from any party to the arbitration agreement regarding jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal, subject to fulfilling the conditions set out in sub-section (2) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act. Thus, a petitioner, who has invoked section 20 of the Arbitration Act, is under a mandatory obligation to satisfy the High Court Division that all the conditions stipulated in clauses (a) to (c) of section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act are satisfied before entertaining or registering an application. In other words, the power invested in the High Court Division for entertaining an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act is not an independent power, for, it can be exercised by the High Court Division only upon being satisfied that (a) the determination of the question is likely to produce substantial savings in costs, (b) the application was submitted without any delay and (c) there is good reason why the matter should be decided by the Court. Therefore, the High Court Division's power having been circumscribed by section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act, an application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act should be taken into account by the Court only after being satisfied as to fulfilling the conditions set out in clauses (a) to (c) of section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act. Additionally, the petitioner is also required to state the reasons/arguments/grounds, based on which the High Court Division would dispose of the application.</u>

34. From a meticulous scrutiny of the averments made in this application and careful examination of the annexed papers, I did not find that filing of the instant application before the High Court Division helped the petitioner or the respondents to save costs, nor did I find that the application was filed without squandering time inasmuch as the interim Order was passed by the arbitral tribunal on 2-8-2018, whereas the present application has been filed on 30-8-2018, save and except finding that the petitioner has placed before this Court some reasons as to why the question of jurisdiction should be adjudicated upon by this Court. However, section 20(2) of the Arbitration Act requires that the petitioner must simultaneously satisfy all the three conditions laid down in clauses (a) to (c) thereof, for, none of the clauses (a) to (c) ends up with the word 'or'. Since the petitioner has failed to satisfy this Court about how he is saving costs by invoking the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act and, also, since the petitioner approached this Court after nearly one month of passing the interim Order of the arbitral tribunal, I find that the petitioner ought to have challenged the jurisdiction of the tribunal before the arbitration tribunal. Therefore, this Court is led to hold that the instant application cannot be entertained for adjudication upon the question of jurisdiction of the tribunal and the interim Order passed by this Court at the time of admission of this matter on 3-9-2018, is liable to be vacated. Furthermore, in view of the stipulations made in sub-section (4) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act by the Legislature that "unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section, the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award", the arbitral tribunal is under an obligation to continue with the arbitration proceedings towards disposing of the arbitration pending before it.

35. The seventh issue is whether the petitioner has waived his right to challenge the appointment of the arbitrators and, also, whether he has waived his right to object to the impugned interim Order. The above issue has to be framed by this Court in order to address the submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 4 with reference to the provisions of section 6 of the Arbitration Act and the case of Joinal Abedin Jamal vs Noor Afzal, 63 DLR 432. Let .me, therefore, see the provisions of section 6 of the Arbitration Act, which run as follows:

6. Waiver of right to object—A party who knows that—

(a) any provision of this Act from which the parties may derogate, or

(b) any requirement under the arbitration agreement, has not been complied with and yet proceeds with the arbitration without stating his objection to such non-compliance without undue delay or if a time limit is provided thereof within such period of time, shall be deemed to have waived his right to so object.

<u>36. From a careful reading of the provisions of section 6 of the Arbitration Act, it appears to this Court that when a party before the arbitral tribunal does not raise any objection with regard to non-compliance of any provision of the Arbitration Act or with regard to non-fulfillment of any requirement set out in the arbitration agreement within the time prescribed in the Arbitration Act and/or within the time-limit stipulated in the arbitration agreement or, in the absence of any stipulation as to the time in the law or in the arbitration agreement, within a reasonable time without making any delay, for dealing with that scenario, the Legislature mandated the arbitral tribunal and the Courts to take a presumption that the aforesaid party has waived his right to so object.</u>

37. The crucial aspect of the provisions of section 6 is, thus, the time to raise such objection, which is required to be prescribed either in the law or to be stipulated in the arbitration agreement. Since in this case, the petitioner is raising question about appointment of arbitrators towards the formation of the arbitral tribunal in question, the respondents are taking a plea that the petitioner, by not raising the objection immediately after knowing about the appointment of the arbitrators or soon after passing the impugned interim Order dated 2-8-2018, has waived his right.

38. Upon skimming through the provisions (a) relating to appointment of arbitrators, (b) regarding raising challenge as to holding the position of the arbitrator and (c) about raising question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal, it appears to this Court that no time-frame is prescribed in the law for raising an objection as to appointment of the members of the arbitral tribunal, nor is there any such stipulation in the arbitration agreement executed by the partners of the MSC (the petitioner and the respondent No. 4) and, therefore, the only tool to assess the time limit is whether the petitioner has made undue delay in raising objection as to the appointment of arbitrators and formation of the arbitral tribunal. This Court's view is that since the parties to the ongoing arbitration proceedings are yet to file their respective written pleadings before the arbitral tribunal, there has not been any such delay in raising the objection as to appointment of the arbitrators or as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal which can be termed as undue or unreasonable. In the cited case of Joinal Abedin Jamal vs Noor Afjal, 63 DLR 432, the aggrieved party raised objection as to appointment of the arbitrator after passing the award by the arbitral tribunal, and that too before the Execution Court, which led this Court to hold that by not raising the objection as to the appointment of the arbitrator before the arbitral tribunal within a reasonable time, the Court deems that the party has waived his right to raise such objection as to the appointment of arbitrators or jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal.

39. I would finally take up the last three issues, being issue Nos. viii, ix and x, together for the sake of their better resolution. The issues are whether the present Members and the Chairman of arbitral tribunal should continue to perform their functions, whether this Court should constitute/create a new arbitral tribunal and whether the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 pending before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka should be kept in abeyance, so that the new arbitrators may review the impugned interim Order passed by the arbitration tribunal on 2-8-2018. The above issues have been framed by this Court to consider the suggestions proposed by the arbitrators before this Court.

40. In order to deal with these three issues, I need to sum up the findings made by this Court hereinabove. The findings of this Court on the 7 (seven) issues so far dealt with by this Court are: (a) there is existence of an arbitration agreement between the partners of the MSC (i.e. between the petitioner and the respondent No. 4) and they are bound to resolve their dispute through the arbitration, (b) the arbitral tribunal is a valid one and the tribunal lawfully passed the impugned interim Order, (c) for resolution of the petitioner's grievance, the apparent fora are either the arbitral tribunal for invocation of the provisions of section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act and section 17 of the Arbitration Act or the High Court Division for seeking a ruling on the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal under section 20 of the Arbitration Act, (d) the petitioner's instant application under section 20 of the Arbitration Act cannot be entertained by this Court, (e) the petitioner has not waived his right to object to the appointment of arbitrator nor has he waived his right to raise objection as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and (f) the Court of District Judge is not competent to hear and adjudicate upon the issues of appointment of arbitrators or jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal. Now, the only option remains for the petitioner to go back to the arbitral tribunal and file application before it either under section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act or under section 17 of the Arbitration Act.

<u>41. After delivering of the Judgment with regard to the core issues of this case, namely, issue Nos. (i) to (vii), this Court expressed its opinion in the open-Court addressing the parties of this case that although this Court has held hereinbefore that the tribunal has been formed lawfully and the interim Order passed by the said tribunal is also valid, however, this Court is going to afford this petitioner Mr Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto) an opportunity to approach the tribunal with an application for reviewing the tribunal's Order dated 2-8-2018. At this juncture, this Court reminded both the parties that as per the prayers of both the parties this Court has adjudicated upon the core issues. Now, it is up to the parties to resolve the dispute either through the arbitral tribunal constituted by the present arbitrators or through reconstituting the arbitral tribunal as per the suggestions put forward by the arbitrators when they appeared before this Court. This Court opined that it would be fair for all the parties if the tribunal is reconstituted with one nominated person from each of the side and the Chairman is appointed by this Court. If they wish to resolve the dispute through a reconstituted arbitral tribunal by appointing any one from the concerned arbitrators, they must first take consent from the present arbitrator/s and, in the event that s/he would be comfortable to work with the newly appointed members and Chairman, only then his/her name may be proposed by the parties as the member of the reconstituted tribunal. In reply thereto, after consulting with the present arbitrators and also receiving the instructions from their respective clients, Mr Tanvir Parvez, the learned Advocate for the petitioner proposes the name of Mr Debborata Laha, son of Promode Chandra Laha and Maya Rani Banik, RM Center (4th Floor), 101 Gulshan Avenue, Dhaka-1212 (Contact: 019-7800-4545) as the arbitrator of the petitioner, Mr Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto) and Ms. Faria Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 4, proposes the name of Mr Afzal Husain Choudhury, son of late Abul Hossain Choudhury, House No. 55, Road No. 4A, Dhanmondi, Dhaka-1209 (Contact: 017-1400-4587) as the arbitrator of the respondent No. 4, Mr Zahed Obaidul Huq Chowdhury. Pursuant to obtaining two names from the two sides, this Court asked both the sides as to whether they wish to appoint the Chairman of the tribunal from the retired Hon'ble Chief Justices or from the former Hon'ble Judges of either Division of the Supreme Court or from the learned Advocates of this Bar. It was notified to them that an Hon'ble Chief Justice (retired) should be remunerated more or less Taka 25,00,000 (twenty five lacs) and an Hon'ble Judge (retired) of either Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh should not be paid less than Taka 10,00,000 (ten lacs). They opted to appoint a former Hon'ble Chief Justice. This Court then announced Mr Md Muzammel Hossain, the former Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh, as the Chairman of the arbitral tribunal.</u>

42. Upon arriving at the above consensus through taking necessary consents and instructions from the partners of the MSC and the present arbitrators, this Court is of the view that the present application may be disposed of with a direction upon the District Judge Court, Dhaka outlining his next course of action with regard to the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 and, also, upon the arbitral tribunal as to the time-limit for conclusion of the arbitration proceedings.

43. The Arbitration Application No. 14 of 2018 is, thus, disposed of without any order as to costs with the following observations, Orders and directions; (i) Since the interim Order dated 12-8-2018 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 has already expired, there is no need to pass any Order for staying its operation. In other words, the interim Order dated 2-8-2018 shall not be enforced until the same is endorsed by the reconstituted arbitral tribunal.

(ii) The learned Advocates for both the sides are hereby directed to notify their respective parties regarding appointment of the Chairman of the reconstituted arbitral tribunal. They are further directed to contact Mr Justice Md Muzammel Hossain, the former Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh (017-8766-2239) and supply him a copy of this Judgment, so that he can take necessary preparation towards having first sitting of the reconstituted tribunal with the members at his earliest convenience.

(iii) The learned District Judge, Dhaka shall not proceed with the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 under section 21(4) of the Arbitration Act till receiving an Order from the reconstituted arbitral tribunal on the application proposed to be filed by Mr Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto) for reviewing the interim Order dated 2-8-2018 passed by the arbitral tribunal.

(iv) The reconstituted arbitral tribunal shall be completely free and independent to hear the application proposed to be filed by Mr Ghulam Mohiuddin (Bhutto) and to pass an appropriate Order on that application for reviewing the interim Order dated 2-8-2018.

(v) If the said interim Order dated 2-8-2018 is kept intact by this reconstituted arbitral tribunal, in that event, the learned District Judge shall resume its functions to deal with the proceedings of Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018, and in the event the reconstituted arbitral tribunal modifies/alters the said Order dated 2-8-2018, in that event, the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 shall stand dismissed. However, in that scenario, the respondent No. 4 shall submit a certified copy of the arbitral tribunal's Order before the Court of District Judge, Dhaka, which shall, thereupon, close the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 501 of 2018 recording an appropriate Order.

(vi) The arbitral tribunal shall endeavor to commence the proceeding formally at the end of September, 2019 and, thereafter, put in its best efforts to conclude the arbitration proceedings preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of its formal commencement.

Office is directed to send a copy of this Judgment to Mr Justice Md Muzammel Hossain, the former Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh and to the learned District Judge, Dhaka at once for their information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
Sudipta Arjun, Advocate -------- For the Petitioner. 
ASM Nazmul Haque DAG with Afifa Begurn Swapna AAG -------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Mujibur Rahman (Md) ---------- Petitioner
VS
Arpita Sampatti Prattyarpan Appeal Tribunal, Sylhet and 7 (seven) others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
