In the present case in hand it appears that the petitioner in the disguise of Article 102 of the Constitution trying to enforce the provisions of RPO. In the present case in hand it further appears that the question as raised by the petitioner regarding certain declarations made by the respondent No.7 before the Election Commission which is completely a dispute to be resolved by the competent authority as provided in the Represented People Order (RPO). Admittedly there is a provision namely Article 12 of the RPO to deal with the issue as raise herein.

343. The question as relates to the date of release of the incumbent MP from jail and the period of sentenced served out by him has been raised in the present case in hand. I have carefully examined the papers and documents as well as numerous materials submitted before this Court. On careful analyses of the same it appears that a series of disputed questions of fact has been raised while dealing with the said issue. The claim of the petitioner was vehemently opposed by the respondents including the respondent No.7. In course of hearing before this Court numerous affidavits were filed as well as papers and documents were submitted. So it appears that a serious dispute has been raised regarding the same. The deliberations and the contentions as raised herein clearly shows that the same falls within the established principle of, “Disputed Question of Fact.” The contentions as raised by the petitioner and the respondents requires elaborate investigation as well as it also requires examination, as production of evidence and also the question of examination and cross examination of witnesses. As such I am of the view that since serious disputed question of fact has been raised the same cannot be addressed in a summary proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh.

“Constitution of Bangladesh, 1972-Article 102(2)Public Interest Litigation-The parameters within which the High Court Division should extend its discretionary jurisdiction in entertaining a PIL.

1. Before entertaining a petition the Court will have to decide the extent of sufficiency of interest and the fitness of the person invoking the discretionary jurisdiction.

2. The court which considering the question of bonafide in a particular case will have to decide as to why the affected party has not come before it and if it finds no satisfactory reason for non appearance of such affected party, it may refuse to entertain the petition.

3. If a petition is filed to represent opulent members who were directly affected by the decision of the Government or Public Authority, such petition would not be entertained.

4. The expression ‘person aggrieved’ used in Article 102(1) means not any person who is personally aggrieved but one whose heart bleeds for the less fortunate fellow beings for a wrong done by any person or authority in connection with the affairs of the Republic or a Statutory Public Authority.

5. If the person making the application on enquiry is found to be an interloper who interferes with the action of any person or authority as above which does not concern his is not entitled to make such petition.

6. The Court is under an obligation to guard that the filing of a PIL does not convert into a publicity interest litigation or private interest litigation.

7. Only a public spirited person or organization can invoke the discretionary jurisdiction of the Court on behalf of such disadvantaged and helpless persons.

8. The Court should also guard that its processes are not abused by any person.

9. The Court should also guard that the petition is initiated for the benefit of the poor or for any number of people who have been suffering from common injury but their grievances cannot be redressed as they are not able to reach the Court.

10. It must also be guarded that every wrong or curiosity is not and cannot be the subject matter of PIL.

11. No petitions will be entertained challenging the policy matters of the Government, development works being implemented by the Government, Order of promotion or transfer of public servants, imposition of taxes by the competent authority.

12. The Court has no power to entertain a petition which trespasses into the areas which are reserved to the executive and legislative by the Constitution.

13. A petition will be entertained if it is moved to protect basic human rights of the disadvantaged citizens who are unable to reach the Court due to illiteracy or monetary helplessness.

h) Petitions from riot victions.

Therefore, when the writ petitioners challenged the continuation of the appellant on the ground of his not belonging to a particular caste what they in fact challenged is the validity of the election of the appellant, though apparently the petition is for the writ of quo-warranto.

It seems that in this case, the High Court has gone out of its way, firstly in relying on the Xerox copies of the service records of the appellants and then at the appellate stage, in calling the first of the Electricity Board where the appellant was working . Again merely because the appellant was described as being a Christian in the service records did not mean that he appellant was actually a person professing Christian religion. It was not after all known as to who had given those details and further as to whether the details, in reality, were truthful or not. It would be unnecessary for us to go into the aspect whether the petitioner in reality is a Christian for the simple reason that this issue was never raised at the time of his election. Again the appellant still holds the valid caste certificates in his favor declaring him to be belonging to Scheduled Caste and further the appellant’s status as the Scheduled Caste was never cancelled before the authority under the 1993 Act which alone had the jurisdiction to do the same. If it was not for High Court to entire into the disputed question of fact regarding the caste status of the appellant, the findings recorded by it on that question would lose all its relevance and importance. There is one more peculiar fact which we must note. It has come in the judgment of the learned Single Judge as also in the Division Bench that the appellant ‘converted’ to Christianity. Now, it was not nobody’s case that the petitioner ever was converted nor was it anybody’s case as to when such conversion took place, if at all it took place. It was further held that, “If it was for High Court to enter into the disputed question of fact regarding the caste status of the appellant, the findings recorded by it on that question would lose all its relevance and importance.”

349. I have also examined the decisions as referred by the learned counsel for the petitioner. On perusal of the same I am of the view that since the Writ Petition is itself not maintainable because of the disputed question of fact as such these are not relevant or considerable in any manner.

350. Regarding writ of quo warranto the fundamental Rule is that the petition has to be in greater public interest. Any such attempt for securing private interest cannot be encouraged. In the case in hand it has been revealed that the petitioner has far reaching personal interest and intends to use this as weapon to defeat his political rival. Apart from that it is now a well settled proposition of law is that if there is any alternative remedy available no writ petition even in the form of quo warranto is liable to be maintained.

351. The proceeding under Art. 102(2) of the Constitution is a summary one and it is decided on the statements made on affidavits filed by the parties and the documents annexed to the application and the affidavit-in-opposition. Hence it is often held that the court will decline to exercise jurisdiction when the application involves resolution of disputed question of fact. The decision reported in 42 DLR(AD) 13 lends support to the above contention. In this summary proceeding examination of disputed question of fact which is a complicated in nature and as a general rule cannot be undertaken nor investigation of title to property made and it is neither desirable nor advisable to enter into the merit and record a finding as to disputed question of fact. The decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 232 lends support to the above order. The court will neither decide the complicated question of title nor disputed questions of fact relating to damages or compensation.

352. The rule is that the court will decline to exercise the jurisdiction only when the dispute as regards facts is such that the dispute cannot be reasonably resolved on the facts pleaded and documents produced before the court. The decision reported in 19 DLR (SC) 228 lends support to the above order.

353. In the instant writ petition it clearly transpires that the contentions as raised by the parties can only be determined by adjudication of the factual aspects and for that a detailed investigation is requires which includes examination of evidence as well as examination of witnesses. The contentions as raised thus are highly disputed question of facts which in the line of the above authorities cannot be adjudicated in a summary proceedings under Article 102 of the Constitution of the republic.

354. Considering the facts and circumstances, discussion made hereinabove as well as the decisions as referred to, I am of the view that the instant writ petition is not maintainable.

355. Accordingly the Rule is discharged. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Tariq-ul-Hakim J: This Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 25-1-1996 (Annexure-G) passed by the respondent No.2 in LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to release 283/4 decimals of land belonging to the petitioner out of plot No. 1059 MRR Khatian No. 340 of Mouza Shamsharabad, Lakshmipur due to abatement of LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 and publish the same in the official Gazette and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioners claim to have purchased an area of 283/4 decimals of land in Mouza Shamsharabad, Lakshmipur within the municipality appertaining to plot No. 1059 MRR Khatian No. 340 in the District of Lakshmipur from its recorded owners by registered kabala Nos. 10230-10231 dated 6-5-1984 and kabala Nos. 3786-3789 dated 20-3-1991. The petitioners after purchasing the aforesaid land constructed residential houses there in accordance with the approved plan after obtaining necessary permission from the local municipality and are residing there. In the meantime, beyond the knowledge of the petitioners LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 dated 5-4-1994 was started for the acquisition of an area of 1.46 acres of land including the petitioner's aforesaid land for extension of the Lakshmipur Sadar Hospital. Subsequently, it came to the knowledge of the petitioner that notices under sections 3 and 6 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 hereinafter "the Ordinance", was served upon the petitioner's predecessors-in-interest, the vendors of the land Lalit Mohan Pal and others in whose names the records of rights were prepared, fixing 9-7-1994 for objection hearing. The petitioners thereafter filed their objections with the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur and although the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Lakshmipur made his award of compensation on 18-7-1994 as per section 7(3) of the Ordinance, the petitioners have not received any compensation. On 10- 10-1995, the petitioner No. 1 filed an application with the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur which was numbered as Petition No. 737 of 1995 giving rise to Miscellaneous Case No. 4 of 1995-1996 praying for publishing a Gazette notification declaring abatement of the LA proceedings pursuant to section 12 of the Ordinance, for non- compliance of the provision of section 10 of the Ordinance, but the same was rejected by the respondent No.3, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Lakshmipur by the impugned order. The learned Advocate for the petitioner thereafter served a Notice of Demand for Justice to the respondents to publish a Gazette notification declaring abatement of LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 in respect of the land in possession of the petitioners but the respondent No.2 by his letter dated 24-4-1996 refused to do so. Thereafter, the petitioner No. 3 was served with a notice on 23-4-1996 (Annexure-K) from the Office of the respondent No. 2 to vacate the aforesaid premises.

3. Being aggrieved, the petitioners have come to this Court and obtained the present Rule.

4. It is stated that the decision to acquire land by the aforesaid LA proceedings was finalised by the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur on 12-6-1994. Thereafter, the requiring body made the money available to the Deputy Commissioner on 8-6-1995 for payment of compensation to the affected persons. The same was however, not paid to them and was deposited in the RD account on 2-3-1996 i.e. after one year and nine months. Thus compensation money having been deposited in the RD Account within one year of final decision of acquisition has resulted in a breach of section 10(2) of the Ordnance, and the Deputy Commissioner is required to make a Gazette notification that the acquisition proceedings have become abated.

5. The respondent No. 1, Government of Bangladesh, is contesting the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition and a Supplementary Affidavit denying the materiel allegations. It has been stated, inter alia, that LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 was started on 12-6-1994 and all the steps were taken in accordance with law; It has been further stated that the compensation money was made available by the requiring body to the Deputy Commissioner on 8-6-1995 vide Memo No. 119(8) of the Ministry of Health and Family Planing which is well ahead of the statutory period of one year and that no question of abatement of the LA proceeding arises. It has been further stated that the land in question has already been handed over to the requiring body and that the petitioners cannot have any claim on it and that the Rule is liable to be discharged.

6. Mr Mihir Kanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, had drawn our attention to the order sheet and records of LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 and submits that the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur gave his final approval for acquisition of the petitioners' land on 6- 6-1994 and that the compensation money after being made available to the Deputy Commissioner's Office and after being offered to the affected persons was deposited in the RD Account on 2-3-1996 i.e. almost one year nine months after the final decision for acquisition of the petitioner's land was taken by the Government and therefore, the LA proceedings in respect of the petitioners' land will be deemed to have been abated and that in accordance with sections 10 and 12 of the Ordinance the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur is required to make a declaration to that effect in the official Gazette. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate has drawn our attention to the decision in Bangladesh vs Subash Chandra Das and others reported in 46 DLR (AD) 63 as well as the decision in the case of Subash Chandra Das vs Bangladesh 50 DLR (AD) 106.

7. As against this, Mr Adilur Rahman Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondents, submits that the petitioners have not been able to show that they have any locus standi to file this Writ Petition and, as such, the Rule is not sustainable. He further submits that the one year period referred to in sections 10 and 12 is the period within which the requiring body is to make the funds available to the acquiring body i.e. the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur and in this case the requisite time has been complied as the requiring body i.e. Ministry of Health and Family Planning, deposited money to the Deputy Commissioner's Office on 8-6-1995. He finally submits that the concerned land has been acquired for a public benefit for construction and extension of Lakshmipur Sadar Hospital and the said land has already been handed over to the requiring body who has utilised the same for the concerned purpose and therefore, in the public interest also the impugned order does not call for interference by this Court and prays that the Rule may be discharged.

8. On perusal of the impugned order and the LA Case records it appears that the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur gave final approval for acquisition of 1.46 acres, of land for the purpose of construction and extension of Lakshmipur Sadar Hospital on 6-6-1994. The respondent No. 1 with his Affidavit-in-Opposition and Supplementary Affidavit has annexed copies of the order sheet of LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 which shows that the Ministry of Health and Family Planning vide memo dated 119/1 (8) made available requisite funds to the Office of the Deputy Commissioner on 8-6-1995 for acquisition of land. Certified copy of the order sheet of the aforesaid LA Case annexed to the Writ Petition shows that notice to the affected persons for receiving compensation money was issued on 27-9-1995; thereafter on 2-3-1996 order was passed for depositing unpaid compensation money in the RD Account maintained by the Office of the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur. Thus it appears that money was deposited into the RD Account more than one year eight months after the final decision to acquire the concerned land by the Deputy Commissioner was taken. Section 10 of the Ordinance is as follows:

10. Payment of Compensation;

(1) On making an award under section 7, the Deputy Commissioner shall, before taking possession of the property, tender payment of the compensation awarded by him to the persons entitled thereto according to the award, and shall, unless prevented by some one or more of the contingencies mentioned in sub-section (2), pay it to them within sixty days from the date of deposit by the requiring person of the estimated amount of compensation under section 7(3).

(2) If the persons entitled to compensation do not consent to receive it, or if there be no person competent to receive the compensation or if there be any dispute as to title to receive the compensation or as to the apportionment of it, the Deputy Commissioner shall keep the amount of the compensation in a deposit account in the Public Account of the Republic which shall be deemed payment for the purpose of taking over possession of the property without any prejudice to the claim of the parties to be determined by the Arbitrator;

Provided that any person admitted to be interested may receive such payment under protest as to the sufficiency of the amount:

Provided further that no person who has received the amount otherwise than under protest shall be entitled to make any application under section 28:

Provided further that herein contained shall affect the liability of any person who may receive the whole or any part of any compensation awarded under this part to pay the same to the person lawfully entitled thereto."

9. The aforesaid provision of law requires the Deputy Commissioner to award compensation to the affected persons before taking possession of the property unless prevented by a dispute as to title to receive compensation or the persons entitled to compensation refuses to receive it or if there is none to receive the same the said amount is to be kept in the public account of the Republic which shall be deemed payment for the purpose.

10. Section 12 of the aforesaid Ordinance is as follows:-

12. Abatement or revocation of acquisition proceeding:

(i) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case the estimated amount of the award of compensation has not been deposited by the requiring person for acquisition of any property under section 5 within the period specified in section 7(4), all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the official Gazette.

(2) The Deputy Commissioner may, with the prior approval of the Government, by notification in. the official Gazette, revoke all proceedings in respect of acquisition of any property at any time before the payment of compensation.

(2) When any proceedings stand abated or are revoked, the Deputy Commissioner shall make an award determining the amount of compensation due for the damage suffered by the owner in consequence of the notice or of any proceedings thereunder and the costs reason- ably incurred by him in the prosecution of the proceedings under this part relating to the said property and shall pay the compensation accordingly. "

1<u>1. The aforesaid section of law provides that if compensation has not been paid or deposited within a period of one year from the date of decision of the Government of acquisition, proceedings in respect of acquisition shall stand abated and a declaration to that effect to be published in the official Gazette by the Deputy Commissioner. In the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration vs Subash Chandra Das & ors reported in 46 DLR (AD) 63, the Appellate Division held-</u>

<u>"The provision of section 12 will come into play only when the compensation is not paid or not kept in deposit account under section 10(1). Under section 12 no obligation, as such, is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation within six monthsfrorn the date of decision for acquisition."</u>

<u>In the said case Mr Justice MH Rahman said:</u>

<u>"Compensation has not been paid or deposited within six months from the date of decision for acquisition in sub-section (1) of section 12 is to be understood with reference to section 10."</u>

<u>His Lordships also said:</u>

<u>"Payment of compensation referred to for the purposes of the Ordinance is that as referred to under sections 10 and 12 i.e. the money that has to be paid by the Deputy Commissioner to the affected persons and not that which has to be paid by the requiring body to the acquiring body".</u>

12. This matter has been further reiterated by Justice Mustafa Kamal, in the same case in the following terms:

"The Deputy Commissioner has to tender and pay compensation to "the persons interested" before taking possession, to be assessed in terms of sections 8 and 9: The payment of compensation is regulated by section 10(1). It is either "paid" in terms of section 10(1) or "deposited" in terms of section 10(2). It is this "payment" and "deposit" in section 1 0 which is attracted in section 12, not the deposit of compensation by the requiring body."

13. In the case of Subash Chandra Das vs Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 106. Mr Justice ATM Afzal delivered judgment as follows:

"An acquisition proceedings shall stand abated if compensation has not been paid or deposited within six months (now one year) from the date of the decision of the authority concerned for acquisition of the property."

14. Thus, from the aforesaid decisions it appears that the compensation money is to be deposited in the RD Account within one year of the decision failing which declaration has to be published in the official Gazette by the Deputy Commissioner that the acquisition property is abated. In the instant case, money was deposited after one year of taking final decision regarding acquisition proceeding. Thus, in our opinion, the whole proceeding is abated.

<u>15. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has submitted that the, petitioner has no locus standi to file the instant writ petition. It appears that these petitioners are all from the same family as they seem to be the son or daughter or wife or husband of one another. It has been also stated that they purchased the' land by registered deeds from the persons who received notices under section 3 of the Ordinance for acquisition proceedings. (Annexure- C) Chairman, Municipality gave permission to the petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 to construct a pucca building and homestead proposed to be acquisitioned. Annexure- K is a notice dated 23-4-1996 addressed to the petitioner No. 3 for vacating the concerned land. Thus, in our view, the petitioners have sufficient interest to file this Writ Petition and" therefore, the learned Deputy Attorney-General's submission that the petitioners have no locus standi is not acceptable.</u>

16. The learned Deputy Attorney-General next submitted that the land has been acquired in LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 for public purpose for construction and extension of the Lakshmipur Sadar Hospital'. According to him, in view of the public interest the acquisition proceedings should not be disturbed. Although we are sympathetic to this submission nevertheless, it cannot be denied that the petitioners' right has been infringed and that a public functionary is required to perform his duties within the strict letter of the law. In the instant case, acquisition proceeding and award of compensation and its refusal ought to have been deposited in the public account within one year which has not been done. In such circumstances, the fact that the land has been acquired for a public benefit is not a sufficient excuse. In our opinion, if the respondents are interested in acquiring the petitioners' land for the public benefit then they ought to make fresh acquisition/requisition proceedings. The present acquisition proceedings of the petitioner's land appears to be hit by section 10 and 12 of the Ordinance.

17. We, therefore, direct the Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur to publish appropriate declaration in the official Gazette that the acquisition proceedings in LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994, so far it relates to the petitioner's land comprising 28% decimals, stands abated.

18. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs.

The impugned order dated 25-1-1996 (Annexure-G) passed by the respondent No.2 in LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the respondents are directed to release twenty-eight and three-fourth, decimals of land belonging to the petitioners in plot No. 1059 MRR Khatian No. 340 of Mouza Shamsharabad, Lakshmipur by declaring in the official Gazette that LA Case No. 34 of 1993-1994, so far as it relates to the petitioner's land, is abated;

End.

lawyer:
Amirul Islam with Dr S Shirin Chowdhury Advocates------ For the Petitioners in all the Writ Petitions.

parties:
Samiran Halder and others ------ Petitioners
vs
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Tariqul-ul-Hakim J: Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Notification bearing Memo Nos. 22.44.1.00.292.2000 (Part-1)-1185 dated 27-12- 2001 and 22.44.1.00.292.2000 (Part-1) dated 28-1-2002 issued by the Director General, Prime Minister's Office purporting to terminate 17 Deputy Assistant Directors (Probationers) from service in alleged exercise of power under Rule 6(2)(a) of the Gazetted Officers (National Securities Intelligence) Recruitment Rules, 1981, (Annexures H and I) should not be declared to have been passed and issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. All these Rules concern common questions of fact and law and are therefore taken up for hearing together and are being disposed of by this single judgment.

3. All the petitioners after obtaining graduation and post-graduation degrees from different Universities of the country were engaged in different jobs but in response to an advertisement published in the Prothom Alo dated 21-3-2000 by the Government of Bangladesh inviting applications for the post of Deputy Assistant Directors in the Directorate under the Prime Minister's Office, applied for the said post and took part in preliminary written and viva voce examinations. Thereafter, appointment letters dated 18-3-2001 were issued by a Director of the Prime Minister's Office appointing 60 persons including the Petitioners to the posts of Deputy Assistant Directors in the National Security Intelligence (NSI) , Directorate in the national pay scale of Taka 4300-185 x 7-5595-EB-195 x 11-7740. The appointment would stand cancelled if the candidates were found unfit in medical examination or if any adverse information is found on police verification or if the officer married or promised to marry a foreign national. Initially, all candidates were to complete a two-year probationary period and the service of the officers would be subjected to the Rules, Regulations and Orders of the Government relating to the service.

4. After completing all formalities the Deputy Director (Administration) in the Director General's Office appointed the petitioners as Deputy Assistant Directors and directed them to report to the training school for 24 months' Commandant Training. In the midst of their training they were posted to different places. Thereafter, by the impugned Memo Nos. 22- 44.1.00.292.2000 (Part 1) 1185 dated 27-12-2001 and 22.44.1.00.292.2000 (Part 1) dated 28-1-2002 issued by the Director General, Prime Minister's Office, the services of the petitioners were terminated in exercise of power under rule 6(2)(a) of the Gazetted Officers (National Securities Intelligence) Recruitment Rules, 1981 on the ground that the performance of the said Officers in various examinations in the Senior Basic Intelligence Course 1/2001 was unsatisfactory.

5. It has been stated that the petitioners completed their first phase of training successfully and hence they cannot be terminated on the plea of unsatisfactory performance in the last leg of their training without proper assessment and such termination is nothing but an excuse to victimise the petitioners as part of a bigger plan to deprive the members of the religious minority community. It has been further stated that the termination of service of the petitioners prior to completion of their training on the ground of unsatisfactory performance without any objective assessment is illegal and without lawful authority and liable to be set aside.

6. Being aggrieved, the petitioners have come to this Court and obtained the present Rules.

7. The respondent No. 1 is contesting these Rules by filing Affidavits-in-Opposition denying all the material allegations made in the Writ Petition. It is stated that the petitioners were appointed to the posts of Deputy Assistant Directors in the Directorate of National Security Intelligence as Probationers and as per their service rules and conditions the probationary period was for two years and due to the unsatisfactory and incompetent performance of the petitioners in the Senior Basic Intelligence Course 1/2001 the authority terminated their service in accordance with law which does not entitle the petitioners to get any relief or the relief prayed for. It is further stated that the authority at the probationary period of the petitioners found them inefficient and, as such, their services were terminated as per Rule 6(2)(a) of the Gazetted Officers (National Securities Intelligence) Recruitment Rules, 1981 (hereinafter referred to as the Rules). During their probationary period the authority had the right to terminate any officer as per rule 6(a) of the said Rules. It has been further stated that the authority issued the impugned letters on the basis of the terms of appointment of the petitioners and their performances during their probationary period and that there was no political or religious motive in the mind of the authority for terminating them. It has been further stated that the Writ Petitions are not maintainable in the eye of law since the petitioners did not challenge the vires of any law but only the impugned order of termination of service which comes under terms and conditions of service. It has been further stated that the authority can terminate the petitioners at any time during the probationary period and that there is no hard and fast rule that they can be terminated only at the end of their two years probationary period. It has been further stated that if there had been any illegality in the impugned order of termination, the petitioners being in the Service of the Republic can ventilate their grievances before the Administrative Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, the instant Writ Petitions are maintainable and the Rules are liable to be discharged.

8. Mr Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the petitioners did not complete their training period of two years when their services were terminated that since the final examination of their training was not held till then therefore, no assessment of their performance could have been made and therefore, the termination of service of the petitioners on ground of unsatisfactory performance is arbitrary, vague and without any basis and hence liable to be set aside.

9. The learned Advocate next submits that neither any evaluation report in support of the impugned orders was produced nor were the petitioners informed of any such result or finding or any show cause notice was given to them to explain their position and hence the impugned orders have been passed in gross violation of the principles of natural justice.

10. The learned Advocate next submits that under Rule 6(2)(a) of the Rules the appointing authority has the power to terminate the service of the petitioners only in the event that the "conduct and work of the probationer is unsatisfactory or that he is not likely to become efficient" and in the instant case there is no finding on the records that the petitioners' conduct and work was unsatisfactory or that they were not likely to become efficient and hence their termination is arbitrary and beyond the scope of law.

11. Mr Islam lastly submits that the authority is not empowered to terminate or withhold the service of the petitioners under Rule 6(4) of the Rules if the petitioner fails to pass any examination or undergo any training and, as such, he submits that the impugned Memos should be declared illegal and without lawful authority.

12. As against this, Mr. Adilur Rahman Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No.1, submits that the petitioners were in the service of the Republic and that the instant Rule concerns their terms and conditions of service. He points out that as per the decisions in the cases of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 and Delowar Hossain vs Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120 all disputes relating to terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic are to be adjudicated in the Administrative Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution unless the vires of any law is challenged. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the aforesaid decisions have been affirmed again in the case of Khalilur Rahman ASP, SB, Dhaka vs Kamrul Ahsan and others reported in 11 MLR(AD) 5 = 10 BLC (AD) 193. The learned Deputy Attorney-General therefore, submits that these Rules are not maintainable and if the petitioners are aggrieved they should go to the Administrative Tribunal for appropriate relief and prays that the Rules may be discharged.

13. In reply, Mr Amirul Islam has drawn our attention to Article 44 of the Constitution wherein it has been stated that the right to move the High Court Division in accordance with Article 102(1) of the Constitution is itself a fundamental right and the same cannot be taken away by any enactment or judicial decision.

14. He has also drawn our attention to Article 117(2) of the Constitution where it is stated that "Notwithstanding anything hereinafter contained Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to settle disputes on terms and conditions of service of persons in the Service of the Republic and that after an administrative tribunal is established under this Article, "no Court" shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal and submits that every provision in the Constitution must be read in its own context and that the non obstante clause relates to Chapter II of the Constitution only and not to the entire Constitution. The learned Advocate further submits that in the judgment of the Mujibur Rahman case reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has not been said that the High Court Division does not have any jurisdiction under Article 102 to hear cases relating to service matters. He has also pointed out Paragraphs 48, 49 , 80, 81 and 82 of the judgment in the case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27. The learned Advocate also submits that in the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh the Court took into consideration the cases of SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India reported in AIR 1987 SC 386 ( Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 (Para 2) where the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the High Court to hear disputes and complaints of civil servants and Government employees by the enactment of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 and the constitution of the Administrative Tribunal was upheld. He submits that eleven years later the decision in SP Sampath Kumar vs Union of India has been overruled by the case of Chandra Kumar vs. Union of India reported in AIR 1997 SC 1125 by the Indian Supreme Court and the jurisdiction of the High Courts to enforce fundamental right matters under Articles 226 and 227 of the Indian Constitution even in service matters was restored. Mr Amirul Islam, therefore, submits that the guaranteed right conferred under Article 102(1) along with Article 44 of the Constitution to move the High Court Division for judicial review cannot be limited by conferring a power upon a Tribunal. Even Article 44(2) provides for empowering a Court to enforce fundamental rights and in the face of such provision he submits that even Parliament cannot confer such power upon a Tribunal which is not a "Court". According to him, it is unimaginable that such conferment can be read and assumed by the judgment of a case and that any such assumption is grossly erroneous on the face of it. He therefore, submits that reading the judgment in its proper perspective as well as interpreting the role of the High Court Division for the enforcement of fundamental rights under Articles 102 and 44(2) of the Constitution clearly indicates that the Administrative Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution has no jurisdiction for judicial review. The power of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution is the exclusive domain of the High Court Division and the Tribunal can only play a supplemental role in upholding fundamental rights. He therefore, submits that the instant Writ Petitions are not only maintainable as per the decisions in the aforesaid cases but they have strong merits and that the impugned Memos call for no interference by this Court and that the Rules should be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

15. We have given the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners our anxious consideration. The power of judicial review of administrative action has been conferred upon the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. Judicial review is the power of the Court to issue directions and declare any action of the Government and autonomous body or local authority to be illegal. The Court exercises this power of judicial review on the principle that public functionaries can exercise power only within their due limits and cannot be allowed to exceed the limits of the authority conferred on them by law. Thus the Court exercises this power of judicial review if the decision of the public functionary is malafide or in violation of the principles of natural justice. In other words, the Court tries to see whether the public functionaries act is ultra vires, that is, without jurisdiction. Article 102(1) of the Constitution empowers the High Court Division to strike down any order which infringes the fundamental rights of the citizen conferred by Part III of the Constitution. Article 102(2) of the Constitution empowers the High Court to issue any order of judicial review only when no other alternative efficacious remedy is available. Article 44 of the Constitution entitles any person to apply to the High Court Division for the enforcement of fundamental rights. However Article, 117 of the Constitution clearly stipulates that notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, the Administrative Tribunal will exercise jurisdiction on matters relating to the terms and conditions of the persons in the Service of the Republic pursuant to which the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 was enacted and the Administrative Tribunals were set up to adjudicate the disputes of persons in the Service of the Republic. Article 117(2) of the Constitution states categorically that "no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal". In the case of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 44 DLR (AD) 111 it has been categorically stated that the Administrative Tribunal set up pursuant to Article 117 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh will adjudicate disputes about terms and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic unless the vires of any law is challenged. This has been affirmed in the subsequent case of Bangladesh vs Shafiuddin Ahmed reported in 50 DLR (AD) 27 as well as in the case of Delwar Hossain vs. Bangladesh reported in 52 DLR (AD) 120. In the Mujibur Rahman case in paragraph 77 it has been said that the power of judicial review was not conferred on the Tribunals under clauses (a) (b) and ( c) of Article 117 of the Constitution. This power is the exclusive preserve of the High Court Division under Article 102(1) of the Constitution. Similarly, in the Shafiuddin case it has been pointed out in paragraph 82 that the Tribunal constituted under Article 117 of the Constitution has no power of judicial review under Article 102(2) of the Constitution and that their role is merely supplemental to the role played by the High Court Division. It has been argued that this indicates that persons in the service of the Republic may take their disputes relating to their terms and conditions of service, not only to the Administrative Tribunal but also to the High Court Division by way of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution. In our opinion, the judgment in the Mujibur Rahman case clearly states that in service matters power has been conferred upon the Administrative Tribunal by virtue of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 to adjudicate disputes regarding terms and conditions of service of persons in the Service of the Republic. The High Court's power of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution has not been substituted by the Tribunals. The Tribunals do not have any power of judicial review but have the statutory power of adjudicating the disputes in service matters. Article 102(2) of the Constitution states that the power of judicial review of the High Court Division under the said Article can only be invoked when no other alternative equally efficacious remedy is available. Thus, the remedy available at the Administrative Tribunal pursuant to Article 117 of the Constitution is a bar to the remedy under Article 102(2) of the Constitution. As for the provision for enforcement of fundamental rights, this Court is bound by the decision of the Appellate Division in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh that the Administrative Tribunal has jurisdiction to hear matters of infringement of fundamental right in service matters of persons in the Service of the Republic unless the vires of any law is challenged in which case Article 102 may be invoked. Paragraph 48 of the Mujibur Rahman case states as follows:

"Within its jurisdiction the Tribunal can strike down an order for violation of principles of natural justice as well as for infringement of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, or of any other law, in respect of matters relating to or arising out of sub-clause (a), but such tribunals cannot, like the Indian Administrative Tribunals in exercise of a more comprehensive jurisdiction under Article 323A (see SP Sam path Kumar vs Union of India, AIR 1937 SC 386 (Para 16) and JB Chopra vs Union of India AIR 1987 SC 357 (para2), strike down any law or rule on the ground of its constitutionality. A person in the Service of the Republic who intends to invoke the fundamental right for challenging the vires of law will seek his remedy under Article 102(1), but in all other cases he will be required to seek remedy under Article 117(2)"

16. Although in Article 102(2) of the Constitution it has been stated that in the absence of other alternative efficacious remedy, the said provision under the Constitution may be resorted to in Khalilur Rahman ASp, SB, Dhaka vs Kamrul Ahsan and others reported in 11 MLR (AD) 5 =10 BLC (AD 193 it has been held that merely because the Administrative Tribunal cannot grant ad interim order of injunction that does not confer jurisdiction on the High Court Division to entertain Writ Petition in such matters. In the aforesaid case the principle enunciated in the Mujibur Rahman case and affirmed in Delowar Hossain s case that the Administrative Tribunal created under Article 117 of the Constitution has the exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate in service matters, even when related to fundamental rights, has been reiterated. It has been pointed out that only in the limited cases where the vires of the law is challenged on the ground of its constitutionality a Writ Petition may be maintained.

17. The Bar's eagerness for the High Court Division to have jurisdiction on all cases on service matters under Article 102 of .the Constitution is understandable. The Administrative Tribunal does not have jurisdiction to issue interim orders. The High Court Division, on the other hand, acting under Article 102 of the Constitution has almost unlimited power including the power to temporarily stay the impugned orders. The framers of the Constitution in their wisdom have however provided for the establishment of Administrative Tribunals to adjudicate disputes in service matters in Article 117 of the Constitution. Although we may sympathise with the arguments of Mr Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners that in fundamental rights matters the High Court Division should be the proper forum to adjudicate all cases including service matters, nevertheless, we are bound by the judgment and law laid down by the Appellate Division in Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh and Bangladesh vs Shajiuddin cases. We cannot agree with the submissions of Mr Amirul Islam that the judgments of the Appellate Division in the Mujibur Rahman case as well as Shajiuddin case indicate that disputes of persons in the Service of the Republic with regard to terms and conditions of employment can be settled at the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution.

<u>18. Reading each of the judgments as a whole, it is clear that their Lordships have categorically stated that only when the vires of a law is challenged the matter can be adjudicated by the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution but all other cases of terms and conditions of employment of persons in the Service of the Republic must be adjudicated by the Administrative Tribunals set up under Article 117 of the Constitution.</u>

19. The instant Rules relate to the petitioners' terms and conditions of service and therefore we are of the opinion that they are not maintainable. Since the Rules are not maintainable in this Court's Writ jurisdiction we are not inclined to go into their merits.

Accordingly, these Rules are discharged. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

Writ Petition No. 1 of 1989 Comilla

lawyer:
SR Pal, Senior Advocate with Md. Fazlul Karim, AI Mohammad Ali and Bazlur Rahman Chhana, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.: This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why the order passed on 6.7.1986 by the Respondent No. 2 as contained in Annexures E and El should not be declared as to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. The case of the petitioner as detailed in the application is, that he has got his homestead spreading over in the part of two CS Plot Nos. 3730 and 3731 appertaining to JL No. 63 of Mouza Lakshmipur, Banchanagar, thana and district Lakshmipur. The said plots consist of 0.71 and 47 decimals of land respectively. The petitioner has got Bagan in a portion of plot 3730, a house in a portion of plot No. 3731 and in between the aforesaid 2 plots there is a family graveyard of the petitioner. One of the co-sharers of the said plots made an agreement with the petitioner for sale of his share measuring 0.56 decimals of land. But subsequently sold the same to one influential man of the locality named Munsurul Haque, The petitioner has filed an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act and the said application was allowed on 13.3.1986 in Miscellaneous Case No. 71 of 1981 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur and the decision was upheld by the superior courts. Munsurul Haque thereafter, trespassed into the suit land under pre-emption by forming unlawful assembly and took away the valuable properties and tried to hang up a signboard in the name of Lakshmipur Mahila College. The said College was allegedly started at Banchanagar on 18.4.1984, but has not yet obtained any sanction from the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Comilla. Upon an application under section 144 CrPC by Munsurul Haque a proceeding was started in No. CP No. 160/P No. 106 of 1986 in the Court of Upazila Magistrate, Lakshmipur and the police submitted a final report on 18.3.1986. Thus being failure to grab the property, Munsurul Haque persuaded the local authority to acquire the said land in the name of the said Mahila College. It may be stated here that as a pre-condition for setting up of a college, a minimum quantity of 3 acres of land is necessary for the College praying for affiliation with the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education. But the land sought to be acquired for the College is only 0.56 decimals of land containing graveyard, Bagan and Bhiti land. On 5.7.1986 the Respondent No.2 issued two notices in the Land Acquisition Case No. 9 of 1985-86 in respect of 38 decimals out of plot No. 3730 out of total 0.71 decimal and in respect of 0.18 decimals of plot No. 3731 out of total 0.47 decimals totaling about 0.56 decimal of unspecified land out of 1.18 decimal of land in those two plots describing the land as Bhiti and Bagan; that the said notices did not spell out the purpose for which the land is acquired. The petitioner thereafter moved the Board of Land Administration and Land Reforms and the Board called for the records which was directed to be sent by 15.8.1986 but the notice was issued on 25.9.1986 and it appears that the case was also disposed of in his absence by order dated 16.1O.l986 by the Board. The order of the requisition does not disclose the purpose to be public one and the order of acquisition purports to acquire land containing homestead as well as family graveyard. It is stated that Lakshmipur Mahila College is situated about half a mile away from the instant site and the land sought to be acquired is not consistant with the land as prescribed for requirement of an Intermediate Mahila College. The entire acquisition procedure is the product of malafide and vindictive endeavour of aforesaid Munsurul Haque which is designed to oust the petitioner from his ancestral homestead causing ruination of his entire family. The compensation has not yet been assessed and the petitioner is still in possession the land.

3. The Rule has been resisted by the Respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 4 by filing a combined affidavit-in-opposition denying the allegations in the petition and stating, inter alia. that Lakshmipur Mahila Colloege has been functioning regularly in a tin-shed on the land acquired and it reveals from the statement furnished by the principal of the College against the objection in reply to petition filed by the petitioner before the Minister of Land Administration that 0.36 acres of land affecting the plot Nos. 3730 and 3731 was donated by Dr. Montazuddin Chowdhury, (at present Vice Chancellor of Islamic University, Dhaka) by a registered deed dated 21.4.1985 along with a big tin shed in favour of the College. One Nurul Huda also donated 0.24 acres of land in the aforesaid plots by a registered deed dated 25.7.1985 to the College and the College has been functioning therein since 13.2,1985. The petitioner filed pre-emption case being' Miscellaneous Case No.71 of 1981 in the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge, Lakshmipur for the land purchased by Dr. Montazuddin Chowdhury which was allowed and against the said judgment an appeal was preferred before the District Judge, Noakhali being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 58 of 1986, which is still pending and it is not correct that there is any residential building or shed on the acquired land in question in plot Nos. 3730 and 3731 except big tin shed wherein the College has been 'functioning. There is no graveyard within the land in question but there is graveyard on the southern middle end of plot No. 3731 attached to the side ditch of C & B Road beyond the acquired land in question. It further appears from the records prepared by the land acquisition staff on 24.5.1986 after filed verification that 0.05 acre of Bhiti land covered by College shed, 0.17 acres Bagan land, 0.16 acres Chala land in Plot No. 3730 and 0.18 acre of Chala land in Plot No. 3731 have been affected by the acquisition which was originally recorded in the names of Abdul Karim, Abdul Rahman, Muslim Mia, son of Elahi Baksh, Shamsul Haque Mia, son of Mafizuddin, Mohammad Anwar Baksh son of Noor Mohammad Mia, Abdur Rahim, son of Abdul Ali, Habibur Rahman, son of Abdur Rahim and Helima Khatoon, wife of Abdur Rahim under SA Khatian No. 800 (CS Khatian No. 971) for an area of 0.71 acres in CS Plot No. 3730 and in the names of Noor Mohammad, Osi Mia, Abdur Rahim, son of Abdul Ali, Halima Khatoon, wife of Abdur Rahmim and Habibur Rahman, son of Abdur Rahim for an area of 0.47 acres under SA Khatian No: 784 (CS Khatian No. 941) in plot No. 3731 including some other plots of Mouza Banchha Nagar. The petitioner however, did not submit any claim or objection on receipt of the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance as to ascertain the quantum of his land affected in the plots or reported any facts before the land acquisition staff at the time of joint verification in the field on 24.5.1986 at the initial stage of the proceeding. There is no graveyard within the land acquired. Mr. Monsurul Haque is the principal of Lakshmipur Mahila College which is managed by a governing body. That there was a pressing need for a Mahili College at Lakshmipur and, as such, the College was started in the Poura Shahid Smriti School in 1984 and subsequently shifted to the shed donated by said Dr. Mantazuddin Chowdhury after making necessary repair and reconstruction of the shed by the college authority and about 38. girl students have appeared at the final HSC Examination this year under regular permission from the Board. When litigation was started in respect of the land in question wherein the college has already been established the governing body of the college resolved to go for acquisition of the land to keep the College free from any encumbrance and accordingly, the Principal has submitted a proposal for acquisition in a prescribed manner as per decision of the governing body dated 24.2.1984 and the matter relating to the acquisition of the land was placed before the District Land Allocation Committee, Lakshimpur for discussion and allotment of the land for the establishment of the Lakshmipur Mohila College. And considering public purpose for development of women's education in the district acquisition proceeding has been started vide RC No. 9/5-85 and notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (II of 1982) was duly published on 28.5.1986 at the convenient places including the land in question calling upon objection against the acquisition proposal but neither the petitioner nor anybody of the recorded tenants filed any objection against the acquisition proposal within 15 days or thereafter and the Government vide Order No. General 1/84/102(68) Requisition dated 31.1.1984 accorded approval on 24.6.1986 confirming the acquisition proposal as provided under section 5(1) of the Ordinance. Thereafter notices under section 6 of the Ordinance were served upon the recorded owners on 15.7.1986 and published at the convenient place calling upon to submit interest in the property in question on 23.7.1986. The petitioner received the notice on 15.7.1986 but instead of submission of claim the petitioner filed an objection before the Minister of Land Administration. However, the objection petition was rejected on 16.1O.l986. The college authority has deposited the entire assessed amount to be paid as compensation, Munsurul Haque, the Principal of the College, has got nothing to do in the acquisition proceeding which was however, started in accordance with the provisions of the Acquistion and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance II of 1982. The petitioner resides with his family elsewhere and not on the plots in question. The petitioner is not the recorded tenant in respect of the suit plot and the name of the petitioner did not appear in the Khatian and, as such, has no right, title, interest and possession in the land in question under acquisition. The petitioner has no locus standi to file this writ petition challenging the acquisition of 0.56 decimal of land. The acquisition proceeding has been finalised as long back on 23.4.1988 when the District Land Acquisition Authority took possession of the acquired land by metes and bound after proper demarcation of land and also handed over possession of the same to the College authority on 23.4.1988, On 25.5.1991 the foundation stone of the main building for Lakshmipur Mahila College was laid ceremoniously by the then Deputy Commissioner, Lakshmipur for which the petitioner has filed a contempt case in the High Court Division against the Respondents being Contempt Case No. 3 of 1991 and, as such, the petitioner has full knowledge of the establishment of Lakshmipur Mahila College over the said plots. The Government also sanctioned Taka 31,06,004/85 for construction of two storied science building for the College and the acquisition of the said 0.56 decimal of land in those plots is now a factum valet as the said Mahila college has been functioning in the acquired land which has been acquired for the public purpose.

4. The petitioner filed affidavit-in-reply denying allegations and reiterated the statements made in the petition and further stated that the petitioner purchased 1.68 acres of land out of plot Nos. 3730, 3731 and 3732 of khatian No. 941,946 and 971 being MRR Khatian No. 784, 787 and 800 in his own name and in the names of his eldest son and wife who acquired title, amongst others, by kabala dated 20.11.56 and 3l.11.58 executed by Abdul Karim, a recorded tenant in the GS Khatian, kabala dated 20.11.1955 executed by Abdul Karim and his brother Abdul Alim and the brother of the petitioner also purchased some portion of the suit plots from the CS recorded tenant by kabala dated 9.6.70 executed by Mokbul Ahmed and kabala dated 3.8.70 executed by Md. Ismail and kabala dated 18.7.51 executed by Abdul Karim and they are in possession. The petitioner also got 0.56 acres of land in the said plots by way of pre-emption proceeding against Dr. Montazuddin and his brother Shamsul Islam, the purchasers from the Co- operative Society in Miscellaneous Case No. 71 of 1981 of the court of Subordinate Judge, Lakshimpur. Mr. Munsurul Haque, the principal of the college along with large number of people armed with various weapons, forcibly took possession of the land of the petitioner for which the petitioner filed contempt petition No.3 of 1991 before this Court and the same is awaiting disposal.

5. Mr. SR Pal, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submitted that the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 laid down the procedure providing for publication of preliminary notice of acquisition of property in respect of any property in any locality if needed or likely to be needed for the specific public purpose or in the public interest and shall cause a notice to be published at convenient places in the prescribed form and manner stating the property is proposed to be acquired. Furthermore, the property to be acquired must be specified one for identification with sufficient particulars to indicate definitely which part of the plot is required with adequate description of the property so as to enable the owners or persons interested in the said property to file objection to the acquisition of the property. Mr. Pal elucidated with reference to Annexure-E and El section 6 of the Ordinance provides iliat when the acquiring authority has made a decision for acquisition of property under section 5 or under proviso to section 4(3)(b) as the case may be, the Deputy Commissioner shall cause public notice to be given in the prescribed manner at a convenient place stating that the authority has decided to acquire the property and intend to take possession thereof and that claims to compensation for the compensation for all interest to such property may be made to him. He has also referred to Annexure-A to the petition which are Khatian Nos. 971 and 941 respectively showing plot No. 3730 measuring 0.71 acres and plot No. 3841 measuring 0.90, plot No. 3731 measuring 0.47, plot No. 3732 measuring 0.20 acre and plot No. 3736 measuring 0.03 respectively and submitted that the authority must indicate definitely which part of the land is required by them out of the plot with adequate description sought to be acquired by them so as to notify owner to exact extent of the property sought to be taken and referred to the decision in the case of Sufia Khatun Vs. 'Secretary, Revenue Department & others 20 DLR (SC) 18. Mr. Pal next submitted with reference to the pre-emption case and the proceeding under section 144 CrPC initiated by Munsurul Haque in respect of the acquired land that on failure to get the land has mala fide initiated the proceeding for acquisition and referred to Annexure-G to the petition dated 12.11.1985 showing that the said college has been started in Banchanagar Ahmedia Govt. Primary School scheduled to commence from 7:00 AM to 11:00 AM and submitted that the allegation of running the college on the land in question is contrary to the record and that only in 1991 they sought to trespass into the acquired land for which contempt case No.3 of 1991 was started against Mr. Munsurul Haque and others which is awaiting disposal by this court and with reference to section 96 and sub-section 9 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act it is submitted that right, title and interest in the pre-empted case deemed to have been vested in the petitioner although no formal possession has yet been obtained due to the objection of the college authority. Mr. Pal next submitted that being a co-sharer and admitted pre-emptor of the suit property sought to be acquired and the acquisition proceeding being bad in law as aforesaid and partly being used as a graveyard, the petitioner has locus standi to file the application against the illegal acquisition proceeding.

6.Mr. Shamsul Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Respondents, has submitted that though there may be certain irregularities in describing the property in notices under sections 3 and 6 of Ordinance II of 1982, the respondent college has obtained possession of the acquired land with a specific boundary where the Mahila College is presently running. And, as such, irregularity, if there 'be any, has been cured by subsequent delivery of possession. Mr. Alam next submitted that Dr. Momtazuddin Chowdhury has donated the land and the tin-shed for the college and there being a pre-emption proceeding at the instance of the petitioner in respect of the kabala land, the authority was obliged to initiate the proceeding for the public interest to set up Mahila College on the acquired land and as such there is no malafide. Mr. Alam next submitted that the petitioner not being a recorded owner in Khatian, Annexure A and there being no objection from the recorded tenants as to the illegality in the acquisition proceeding, the petitioner has no locus standi to challenge the proceeding in this Court.

7. Section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 provides as under.

"3. Publication of preliminary notice of acquisition of property, Whenever it appears to the Deputy Commissioner that any property in any locality is needed or is likely to be needed for any public purpose or in the public interest, he shall cause a notice to be published at convenient places on or near the property in the prescribed form and manner stating that the property is proposed to be acquired:

Provided that no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship, graveyard and cremation ground shall be acquired."

8. Rule 4 of the Acquisition of Immovable Property Rules, 1982 provides that the notices under sections 3, 6 and 7 shall be in forms A, Band C respectively and the notices shall be affixed at convenient places before or near the property sought to be acquired, with copies of such notices displayed in the notice boards of the Collectorate Office of the Upazila (now thana) Revenue office, Tahsil office and office of the Local Parishad or Pourashava within the legal limit of which such property situates.

9. Section 4(1) of the said Ordinance provides for objection against acquisition as under:

"4. Objection against acquisition-(1) Any person interested in any property which has been notified under section 3 as being needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose or in the public interest may within fifteen days after the publication of the notice object to the acquisition of the property."

10. It appears from the aforesaid sections, the relevant rule and the appended forms thereof that the purpose of the issuance of the notices was to intimate the concerned owners or persons to know definitely what part of the land is required out of the big plot of the property sought to be acquired for public purpose, so as to enable them to file objection against the proposed acquisition. In the instant case, as appears from the khatian annexure-A to the petition, that plot No. 3730 in khatian No. 971 comprises 0.71 acres of land and plot No. 3731 in khatian No. 941 comprises 0.47 acres of land and thus the total quantum of land in both the plots is 1.18 acres of land. The copy of the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance in Acquisition Case No.3 of 1985-86 which has been placed before us by the learned Deputy Attorney General go to show the schedule of the acquired land as under:

"Part plot No./Nos 3730, and 3731 Area more or less-0.56 acres. Khatian No. 784, 787 and 800. Mouza Banchanagar, JLN 63 Upazila Lakshmipur, District Lakshmipur. Total area more or less 0.56 acres."

Schedule mentioned in notices Annexures-E and E 1 under section 6 of the Ordinance are as under:

Annexure-E

Schedule

Mouza-Banchanagar,11 No. 63, Upazila &

Zilla-Lakshmipur 	Plot No. Area 	Class

3730 	0.21 	Bhiti

0.17	Bagan

0.38

Annexure-E

Schedule

Mouza-Banchanagar, J.L. No. 63, Upazila &

Zilla- Lakshmipur, Plot No. Area 	Class

3731 	0.18 	Bhiti"

So from both these notices under sections 3 and 6 of the Ordinance, it appears that only 0.56 acres of land has been sought to be acquired out of the bigger plots comprising of 1.18 acres without any specification and demarcation with specific portion out of the said plots.

11. In the cited decision in the case of Sufia Khatoon Vs. Secretary, Revenue Department it is held that:

"It was held by this Court in Ralli Brothers Vs. Province of East Pakistan and others that the Authority requisitioning or acquiring property, under the compulsive power of the Act, must indicate definitely what part of the land is required by them. If they want any specific portion out of a bigger plot, it is necessary that an adequate description of the portion sought to be acquired be given, so as to notify the owner of the exact extent of the property sought to be taken away."

12. In the instant case neither in the notice under seetion 3 nor in any notice under section 6 issued under the Ordinance there was any specific boundary of the acquired land sought to be acquired out of the bigger plots.

13. The learned Deputy Attorney-General also frankly submitted that the notices suffer from vagueness and indefiniteness in description but the same have been cured, according to him, by delivery of possession on specific demarcation to the college authority. It has also been admitted that there was no partition by metes and bounds amongst the co-sharers.

14. From the possession certificate Annexure l(a) it appears that the schedule of land allegedly delivered was CS 3730 and 3731, the land more or less 0.56 acres of Mouza Banchanagar JL No. 63 PS & District Lakshmipur and the same is also vague and indefinite. Such vague description without any specification in the said notices have prevented the persons interested including the petitioner from submitting any effective objection against the acquisition at the initial stage of the acquisition. Thus the petitioner has been deprived of a right or opportunity of being heard and consequently deprived of further enquiry into the matter prior to the report containing the opinion of the authority on the objection as contemplated in section 4 upon issuance of the notice under section 3.

15. It further appears from the record of the proceeding placed before us by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that there is a graveyard in the accquired land. Such land is also exempted from acquisition under the Act and thus the acquisition of case land also suffers from the initial infirmity under the provision of proviso to section 3 of the Ordinance.

<u>16. Thus we are of the view that the description of the land sought to be acquired are vague, indefinite, unspecified and uncertain and did not enable the owners to make an effective objection in writing against the order of acquisition and the same has rendered the acquisition proceeding illegal and not sustainable in law.</u>

17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has not denied the allegations of the Civil and Criminal cases and the results thereof in respect of the acquired land between the petitioner on the one side and the donor of the land and the college authority on the other side. The pre-emption case has been allowed in favour of the petitioner and the decree has been maintained by the superior courts and in the facts and circumstances of the case and the way the various notices were issued, we are of the view that the acquisition proceedings is colorable exercise of powers by the acquiring authority as the respondents 1,2, and 4 had devised this means of circumventing and thwarting a valid decree of the civil Court

18. From the Annexure 'XI series, the sale deeds in favour of the petitioner and judgment in the Miscellaneous case for pre-emption, it appears that the petitioner is the owner of the acquired land on the basis of his purchase from the admitted owners and a co-sharer in the case holding sought to be acquired and has a right to protect his interest against any illegal acquisition of his property.

19. Furthermore, the acquisition proceeding taken against the owners has affected the property and other rights of the owners including the petitioner in the acquired land and, as such, it cannot be said that the petitioner has no locus standi to move this Court against the acquisition proceeding which is tainted with illegality.

20. For the reasons aforesaid, the acquisition proceeding in Acquisition Case No.9 of 85-86 of the respondent No.4 cannot stand in the eye of law and, as such, the order passed on 28.5.1986 issuing notice under section 3 for acquisition of case land in RC Case No.9 of 85-86 and order dated 6.7.86 passed by the respondent No.2 as contained in Annexure-E and El to the petition issued by the respondent No.4 purporting to acquire the land in question are declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

The Rule is accordingly made absolute but without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Tajul Islam Miajee, Advocate—For the Petitioners.
